q: Which sequence is the single loop that every robot, real or simulated, runs?
choices: sense → decide → act → the world changes → sense again
plan the whole motion → act → sense once at the very end
decide → act → stop as soon as the goal has been reached
act → sense → decide only when a sensor reports an error
why: The course reduces every robot to one closed loop: sense, decide, act, the world changes, sense again. A loop that plans once and only senses at the end is open loop, not what a robot runs.

q: According to the course, what is the one engineering reason a robot is split into layers?
choices: Its parts must run at wildly different speeds
Layered code is tidier and easier to read
Each layer is sold by a different robot vendor
ROS 2 forces programs to be split this way
why: "Layers are a consequence of timescales, not of tidiness." A motor must be corrected thousands of times a second; a walking decision need not change more than once a second.

q: Why not write one single program that both corrects the motors and decides where to walk?
choices: It would be both too slow and too twitchy
It would need two separate physics engines
It would no longer run inside MuJoCo
It could not read the IMU's sensor data
why: The guide quotes it directly: one program doing both would be "both too slow and too twitchy": too slow for the motors, too jumpy for the plan. That is why the stack separates by rate.

q: From bottom to top, what is the order of the five layers?
choices: Physics → Robot Model → Middleware → Control & Planning → AI
Robot Model → Physics → Control & Planning → Middleware → AI
Physics → Middleware → Robot Model → AI → Control & Planning
Middleware → Physics → Robot Model → Control & Planning → AI
why: Layer 1 Physics/World, 2 Robot Model, 3 Middleware/Robot OS, 4 Control & Planning, 5 AI/Behaviour. Swapping 1 and 2 is the classic slip: the model is a blueprint, the physics is the world.

q: Which layer is nicknamed "the brainstem" and answers "What should the motors do now?"
choices: Layer 4, Control & Planning
Layer 5, AI / Behaviour
Layer 3, Middleware / Robot OS
Layer 1, Physics / World
why: Layer 4 is the brainstem (PD, IK, trajectories, ZMP/LIPM, WBC, MPC). Layer 5 is the cortex, which answers what the robot should achieve, not what the motors do right now.

q: Layer 3 (Middleware / Robot OS) has which nickname and answers which question?
choices: The nervous system: how do the parts talk?
The blueprint: what is this robot made of?
The cortex: what should the robot achieve?
The body's reality: what do forces do?
why: Middleware is the nervous system: transport, interface contracts, time, logging between programs. The blueprint is Layer 2, the cortex Layer 5, the body's reality Layer 1.

q: Complete the course's one-line summary of the stack: "Bottom is ___. Top is ___."
choices: fast and dumb; slow and smart
slow and exact; fast and rough
smart and slow; dumb and fast
hardware only; software only
why: Physics runs at 500 Hz and knows nothing about goals; task planning runs below 1 Hz and is the smartest part. The rates fall as the intelligence rises.

q: Roughly how many orders of magnitude separate the 500 Hz physics step from a sub-1 Hz task plan?
choices: About three
About one
About six
About ten
why: 500 Hz down to ~0.5 Hz is a factor of ~1000, i.e. about three orders of magnitude. That spread is exactly why one program cannot do everything.

q: Which typical rate does the study guide give for Layer 5 (AI / Behaviour)?
choices: About 1 – 50 Hz
About 100 – 1000 Hz
About 500 Hz – 1 kHz+
Static: it never runs
why: Layer 5 runs at ~1–50 Hz (a learned gait policy ~50 Hz, navigation 1–10 Hz, task planning below 1 Hz). 100–1000 Hz is Layer 4; 500 Hz–1 kHz+ is physics; static is the robot model.

q: On the real Unitree G1, what plays the role of Layer 1 (Physics / World)?
choices: Reality itself: nothing computes it
An onboard copy of the MuJoCo engine
The vendor SDK's physics module
The MJCF file stored on the robot
why: "On a real robot there is no physics layer: there is only reality." Gravity is not computed and friction is not a parameter. The MJCF is Layer 2 (the model), not the world.

q: Which of these is NOT something the physics engine (Layer 1) computes?
choices: Which joint angles the robot should aim for
Contact forces and friction at the feet
Actuator dynamics and joint limits
Synthetic IMU readings for the declared sensors
why: Layer 1 computes integration, contact, friction, inertia, joint limits, actuator dynamics and sensor readings. Choosing target angles is a decision: Layer 4 or 5.

q: Which of these is NOT a Layer 1 physics engine?
choices: URDF
PyBullet
Isaac Sim
Gazebo
why: URDF is a robot-model file format (Layer 2, ROS's interchange format). MuJoCo, PyBullet, Isaac Sim/Lab, Gazebo and ODE/Bullet/PhysX are engines or simulators.

q: Why does the course say "contact is the whole game in legged robotics"?
choices: Everything interesting happens where foot meets floor
Contact is the only force that MuJoCo actually computes
Legged robots are judged mainly on how softly they land
Contact sensors are a walking policy's most important input
why: Balance, walking and falling are all decided at the foot-floor contact, which is also the hardest thing to simulate well. The G1 model does not even declare contact sensors.

q: Which pairing of robot-model format and ecosystem is correct?
choices: URDF – ROS, the interchange format
MJCF – Gazebo, the ROS simulator
SDF – NVIDIA Omniverse and Isaac
USD – MuJoCo, our course format
why: MJCF is MuJoCo's (ours), URDF is ROS's and the de-facto interchange format, SDF is Gazebo's, USD is NVIDIA Omniverse/Isaac's.

q: A student says: "The robot model is the simulation part; a real robot doesn't need one." What is the correction?
choices: Real controllers need it: IK needs link lengths, MPC needs dynamics
Correct: a real robot needs only its vendor SDK, its motors and its IMU
Correct: the model exists only to feed numbers to the engine
Real robots need it only to render a 3-D picture for the user
why: The guide calls this a correction worth making early. IK needs link lengths, MPC needs dynamics, estimation needs sensor positions: "The model describes the robot; the engine simulates the world."

q: What does a real G1 carry onboard?
choices: A model of itself, but no world simulator
A world simulator, but no model of itself
Both a world simulator and a self-model
Neither: it runs only learned policies
why: The real-vs-sim table: the real G1 has an onboard kinematic/dynamic model (Layer 2) while Layer 1 is reality itself. Keeping model and engine apart makes Layer 1 vs Layer 2 clear.

q: The G1 has nsensor = 4. What are the four sensors?
choices: A gyro and an accelerometer in each of two IMUs
One foot contact switch under each of four soles
Two head cameras plus two IMUs in the torso
Four joint-torque sensors in the hips and knees
why: Two IMUs (torso and pelvis), each a 3-axis gyroscope plus a 3-axis accelerometer: 4 sensors, 12 numbers. No camera, no joint-torque sensors, no foot contact switches.

q: A controller needs to know when a G1 foot touches the floor. What does the course's G1 model provide for that?
choices: Nothing: no contact sensor is declared, so you must add one
A foot contact switch under each sole, two numbers per step
The IMUs report foot contact as part of their 12 numbers
sensordata lists all eight contact forces every step
why: "A robot cannot sense what its blueprint does not declare." The G1 declares only two IMUs; contact switches, cameras and torque sensors would have to be added to the MJCF.

q: Where does the G1's servo law τ = k_p(ctrl − q) − k_v·q̇ actually run?
choices: Inside mj_step, in the actuator model, so inside f
Inside your policy π, once per 20 ms decision, before mj_step
Inside the sensor function h, after each step
In the middleware, between two processes
why: The position servo is part of the actuator model, computed by the physics engine every timestep, just as a real servo drive closes its own loop below anything you write.

q: On the G1, what is k_p on every joint, and what torque does a 0.1 rad error produce?
choices: k_p = 500 N·m/rad; 50 N·m
k_p = 500 N·m/rad; 5000 N·m
k_p = 200 N·m/rad; 20 N·m
why: k_p = 500 on every joint, so 500 × 0.1 = 50 N·m. 15.8 is the knee's damping k_v, not its stiffness; 200 is the week-1 two-link leg's gain.

q: A G1 position servo (k_p = 500 N·m/rad) is at rest, 0.04 rad short of its command. What torque does it apply?
choices: 20 N·m
2 N·m
why: At rest q̇ = 0, so τ = k_p(ctrl − q) = 500 × 0.04 = 20 N·m. 12,500 comes from dividing 500 by 0.04 instead of multiplying.

q: A servo has k_p = 500, k_v = 10. The error ctrl − q is 0.06 rad and the joint moves at q̇ = +1 rad/s. What torque?
choices: 20 N·m
40 N·m
30 N·m
why: τ = 500 × 0.06 − 10 × 1 = 30 − 10 = 20 N·m. Adding the damper (40) or ignoring it (30) are the typical slips; the damper resists motion, so it subtracts.

q: What does middleware (Layer 3) ultimately buy you?
choices: Modularity: separately written programs act as one robot
Speed: contacts are solved in parallel on many machines
Accuracy: link lengths are measured for you on start-up
Learning: policies are trained from its message logs
why: Transport, interface contracts, time, lifecycle, logging and introspection together buy modularity: perception, control and planning become separable programs.

q: Why does this course deliberately skip ROS 2?
choices: Linux-only, no Colab, and it solves a problem we lack
It is obsolete and no longer used in industry
MuJoCo refuses to run on a machine where ROS 2 is installed
It drives real hardware only, never a simulator
why: ROS 2 is effectively Linux-only, cannot run in Colab, and solves a distributed-systems problem a one-process simulation does not have. The course still says: learn it if you go into robotics.

q: In this course's own stack, what is Layer 3?
choices: A single Python process
A ROS 2 bridge to the vendor SDK
LCM messages between twelve programs
The MJCF file's <actuator> section
why: For one simulated robot, a single Python process is a legitimate architecture. The real G1 uses a vendor SDK plus a ROS 2 bridge.

q: Which technique belongs to Layer 4 (Control & Planning) rather than Layer 5?
choices: ZMP / LIPM walking
Reinforcement-learned gaits
Vision-language-action models
Task planning from a spoken goal
why: Layer 4: PID/PD, IK, trajectory generation, ZMP/LIPM walking, whole-body control, MPC (weeks 2–6). RL, imitation, vision, navigation, task planning and VLAs are Layer 5.

q: Which classification of items into layers is correct?
choices: URDF file → 2; PID gain → 4; PPO → 5
URDF file → 1; PID gain → 3; PPO → 4
URDF file → 2; PID gain → 5; PPO → 4
URDF file → 3; PID gain → 4; PPO → 2
why: A URDF is a robot-model file (Layer 2), a PID gain is classical control (Layer 4), PPO is reinforcement learning (Layer 5).

q: How does a typical learned walking policy actually drive the robot?
choices: It outputs joint targets at ~50 Hz that PD servos track faster
It outputs motor torques directly at 1 kHz, with no servos below it
It replaces both the servos and the physics engine
It rewrites the MJCF gains once at the start of each run
why: A learned policy typically outputs joint position targets at about 50 Hz, and the same classical PD servos track them 10–20× faster.

q: "Learning has won at locomotion, so classical control is now obsolete." What does the course say?
choices: Learning sits on top of classical control; it does not delete it
Correct: learned policies now command raw torques with no servos at all
Correct: only the physics engine is still written by hand
Wrong: learning has not worked for locomotion at all
why: Learning has largely won at locomotion, but the engine, the model, the joint servos and the safety limits are all still hand-written. The policy's targets are tracked by PD servos.

q: A learned policy outputs targets at about what rate, and how much faster do the PD servos track them?
choices: About 50 Hz; servos 10–20× faster
About 500 Hz; servos 2× faster
About 1 Hz; servos 1000× faster
About 1 kHz; servos at the same rate
why: ~50 Hz policy, servos 10–20× faster (500 Hz–1 kHz). On our G1: 50 Hz policy over 500 Hz physics, ten physics steps per decision.

q: Why does a learned walking policy not run inside the 1 kHz servo loop?
choices: It need not: the fast servos chase its targets between decisions
It must, or the robot would fall over in the gap between two decisions
It does: neural networks are fastest in a 1 kHz loop
MuJoCo refuses to call any policy faster than 10 Hz
why: "You cannot put a neural network in a 1 kHz loop, and you do not need to." The slow layer sets the goal; the fast servo layer chases it every physics tick.

q: In x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k), y_k = h(x_k), u_k = π(y_k), which is the only part you write?
choices: π, the policy (Layers 4–5)
f, the world (Layer 1)
h, the sensors (Layer 2)
x, the state (qpos and qvel, 71 numbers)
why: f is the world (mj_step), h is the sensors declared in the MJCF, x is the state. π is your code: the first half of the course writes it by hand, the second half learns it.

q: Which statement about the three-equation loop is true?
choices: The policy sees the state only via h and moves it only via f
The policy reads the state x directly and writes x_{k+1} directly
h is the physics engine and f is the sensor model
u is the observation the sensors report each step
why: "No box can skip another." π gets y = h(x), never x itself, and its action u changes the state only through f. h is the sensors, f the world.

q: On the G1, what are the sizes of the state x, the action u and the observation y?
why: x = qpos + qvel = 36 + 35 = 71; u = ctrl = 29 actuators; y = sensordata = 12 numbers (4 sensors × 3 axes). "The robot is described by 71 numbers but senses only 12."

q: A robot has nq = 23 and nv = 21. How many numbers make up its full state x?
why: The state is qpos plus qvel, so 23 + 21 = 44. Doubling nq (46) assumes qpos and qvel have the same length, which is false whenever there is a free or ball joint.

q: "The G1's declared sensors report all 71 numbers of its state." Is that right?
choices: No: they report 12, so the state must be estimated
Yes: qpos and qvel are copied into sensordata
Yes: the two IMUs measure every joint angle
No: they report none; the policy reads qpos
why: The model declares two IMUs giving 12 numbers. Closing the gap between 12 sensed and 71 state numbers (estimating x from y) is week 6.

q: Physics runs at 1 kHz and a policy at 100 Hz. How many physics steps per decision, and what happens to ctrl in between?
choices: 10; the same ctrl is held and the servos keep correcting
10; ctrl drops back to zero until the next decision
100; the same ctrl is held and the servos keep correcting
0.1; the policy runs faster than the physics does
why: N = f_phys / f_pol = 1000 / 100 = 10 (practice Q2). Between decisions the action is held, and the servo law keeps correcting the joints at every physics tick.

q: Physics runs at 500 Hz and a slower policy at 25 Hz. How many physics steps pass per decision?
why: N = 500 / 25 = 20. 12,500 is multiplying the rates instead of dividing; 0.05 is dividing the wrong way round.

q: Physics runs at 2 kHz and the policy decides once every 25 ms. Physics steps per decision?
why: The physics period is 1/2000 s = 0.5 ms, and 25 ms / 0.5 ms = 50. Equivalently N = 2000 × 0.025 = 50.

q: A physics engine runs at 250 Hz. What is its timestep (period)?
choices: 4 ms
0.4 ms
25 ms
2.5 ms
why: T = 1/f = 1/250 s = 0.004 s = 4 ms. For comparison our G1 runs at 500 Hz, i.e. 2 ms.

q: Between two policy decisions, what keeps correcting the joints?
choices: The servo law, at every physics step
Nothing: the joints coast until the next decision
The policy, re-run on a cached observation
The middleware, replaying the last message
why: The same ctrl is held while the PD law inside mj_step corrects the joints every 2 ms tick. "The slow layer sets the goal; the fast layer chases it."

q: What does a fixed-step integrator pretend happens during one timestep Δt?
choices: Nothing changes during the step
The robot stays in floor contact
Gravity switches off mid-step
The exact answer is already known
why: An integrator turns a derivative into a jump and pretends nothing changes during Δt. That is why a smaller step is closer to reality, and costs more steps per second of robot time.

q: A ball drop simulated at Δt = 0.01 s is 20 mm off after 0.4 s. Using the guide's rule, roughly what error at Δt = 0.002 s?
choices: 4 mm, for five times the work
0.8 mm, for five times the work
4 mm, at no extra computing cost
100 mm, since more steps add error
why: The guide's example: 25× smaller step, 25× smaller error, 25× more work. Here the step is 5× smaller, so the error is 20/5 = 4 mm. 0.8 mm would be a second-order (squared) method.

q: G1 torso height after 3 s from stand: servos off versus servos on?
choices: 0.79 m off, 0.79 m on
why: Disabling actuation drops the torso to 0.134 m; servos on hold 0.792 m. Same physics, same model, same start. (0.142 m is the same fall on Colab; 327 is the weight in N.)

q: Complete the professor's line: "Standing is not a property of the robot. It is a property of the ___."
choices: loop
model
floor
keyframe
why: Nothing about the robot differs between the 0.134 m and 0.792 m runs; only whether a controller is closing the loop.

q: With actuation enabled, you set ctrl = 0 on every G1 actuator and step for 3 s. What happens?
choices: It stands straight-legged at about 0.79 m
It collapses like a rag doll to about 0.13 m
It drops in free fall in about 0.35 s
MuJoCo raises BADQACC and resets it
why: Position servos turn ctrl = 0 into "hold every joint at angle zero", a straight-legged stance they hold at 0.79 m. "Zero command is a command."

q: How do you get a G1 that truly has no controller?
choices: Disable actuation (soc4180.actuation_disabled)
Set ctrl = 0 on all 29 actuators
Delete the stand keyframe from the file
Zero every sensor reading and command before stepping
why: ctrl = 0 is still a command to the position servos. Only disabling actuation removes the controller, and then the torso drops 0.79 → 0.134 m.

q: The limp G1 takes about 1.3 s to drop below 0.2 m, while free fall would take about 0.35 s. Why the difference?
choices: It folds on legs whose feet stay on the floor
MuJoCo's default gravity is weaker than 9.81
The servos still resist it even when disabled
Air drag on the large meshes slows it down
why: The body is not dropped: it pivots and folds on legs planted on the floor, and straight legs buckle slowly at first. Disabled servos produce no torque, and MuJoCo models no air drag here.

q: Ignoring the legs, how long would a body take to free-fall 0.45 m (take g = 10 m/s²)?
why: t = √(2d/g) = √(0.9/10) = √0.09 = 0.3 s. 0.09 s forgets the square root. The real limp G1 is much slower than free fall because its feet stay on the floor.

q: Which set of G1 model counts is correct?
choices: 31 bodies, 30 joints, nu = 29
30 bodies, 29 joints, nu = 30
29 bodies, 36 joints, nu = 35
31 bodies, 36 joints, nu = 36
why: 31 bodies (counting the world), 30 joints (1 free + 29 hinges), 29 actuators, nq = 36, nv = 35, nsensor = 4. 36 and 35 are nq and nv, not joint or actuator counts.

q: What are the G1's mass and weight?
choices: 33.3 kg and 327 N
327 kg and 33.3 N
33.3 kg and 33.3 N
29 kg and 284 N
why: 33.3 kg × 9.81 m/s² ≈ 327 N. Standing still, the contact forces sum to exactly this weight.

q: What are our engine's settings for the G1?
choices: 0.002 s step (500 Hz), implicitfast, g = (0, 0, −9.81)
0.001 s step (1 kHz), implicitfast, g = (0, −9.81, 0) m/s²
why: Timestep 0.002 s → 500 Hz, integrator implicitfast, gravity along −z. 0.02 s is the week-1 timestep that breaks things; +z is up, so gravity is negative z.

q: At the G1's 500 Hz, how many physics steps does a 3 s simulation take?
why: 3 s / 0.002 s = 1500 steps. 167 comes from dividing 500 by 3.

q: Comparing the real G1 with our MuJoCo G1, which layers transfer between the two?
choices: Layers 2–5 transfer; Layer 1 never does
Layer 1 transfers; Layers 2–5 are rewritten
Only Layer 5, the trained policy, transfers
All five transfer if the MJCF is accurate
why: Model, middleware, control and AI can move across; the physics engine is replaced by reality. "That one asymmetry is the sim-to-real problem."

q: Which of these is a source of the sim-to-real gap named in the course?
choices: Real sensors are noisy, biased and late
Real gravity is not 9.81 m/s² indoors
Real robots cannot run PD servo loops
Real joints have no mechanical limits
why: Listed: friction changes with dust and wear, motors saturate and lag, sensors are noisy, biased and late, gearboxes have backlash, real mass is never the file's mass.

q: You set gravity to the Moon's −1.62 m/s² and re-run the limp fall. Which other layers had to change?
choices: None: only Layer 1 changed
Layer 2: rescale every MJCF mass
Layer 4: retune every servo gain
Layer 3: slow the shared clock
why: Gravity is a property of the world. Changing it touches Layer 1 only, which is the point of the exercise: the other layers do not know or care.

q: A 30 kg robot stands still on the Moon (take g = 1.6 m/s²). What do its contact normal forces sum to?
why: Standing still, ΣF_n = m·g = 30 × 1.6 = 48 N. 300 N is its Earth weight (g ≈ 10). The lab shows the G1 on the Moon at about 54 N.

q: Which belief did the course measure and find to be false?
choices: That the G1 falls over with ctrl = 0
That the G1 falls with actuation off
That standing contacts sum to the weight
That one model can serve many data
why: With ctrl = 0 the position servos hold a straight stance at 0.79 m. The other three statements are true and measured.
source: Study guide · How the course fits together

q: What question does the professor want you to ask of any robotics claim, paper or demo?
choices: Which layer is this, and what does it assume beneath it?
How many parameters does the learned policy have?
Was this trained in simulation or on real hardware?
Which physics engine rendered the demo video?
why: "Which layer is this, and what is it assuming about the layers beneath it?" Much robotics hype is a Layer 5 result relying on a Layer 1 that exists only in the lab.

q: "The G1 has nsensor = 4, so its observation y has 4 numbers." What is wrong with this?
choices: Each sensor is 3-axis, so 4 sensors give 12 numbers
Nothing: one number per sensor, 4 numbers in all
nsensor counts IMUs, so there are 4 IMUs, 24 numbers
y is the full state, so it has 71 numbers, not 4
why: nsensor = 4 is two IMUs × (gyro + accelerometer). Each of the four reads 3 axes, so sensordata holds 12 numbers per step.

q: A student shrinks the timestep from 0.002 s to 0.0005 s "for free accuracy". What did it cost?
choices: 4× more steps per simulated second
Nothing: accuracy is free in MuJoCo
4× fewer steps per simulated second
16× more steps per simulated second
why: The step is 4× smaller, so each simulated second needs 4× as many steps (and the error drops about 4×). Smaller is closer to reality and always more work.

q: Which is a reason the course gives for simulating instead of experimenting on a real humanoid?
choices: Learning needs millions of trials, impossible on hardware
Simulation is exact, so policies transfer to hardware unchanged
Simulated sensors are realistically noisy by default
Contact and friction are easiest to get right in sim
why: A real humanoid is expensive, fragile and slow to reset, and learning needs millions of trials; sim is repeatable, faster than real time and parallel. It is not exact, and its sensors are noiseless.

q: Which is listed as a cost of simulating rather than an advantage?
choices: Sensors are noiseless in sim, never in reality
Simulation runs slower than real time
Simulated experiments can never be repeated exactly
Simulation cannot run robots in parallel
why: Costs: contact and friction are hard, actuator limits and delays are often ignored, sensors are noiseless. Speed, repeatability and parallelism are the advantages. The total gap is the sim-to-real gap.

q: What does the name MuJoCo stand for?
choices: Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact
Multi-Joint Controller for robots
Muscle–Joint Coordination model
Multi-body Joint Computation
why: Mu-lti Jo-int dynamics with Co-ntact: an engine built for many joints and contact with the ground. Its XML model format is MJCF.

q: Which MJCF section holds named poses such as the G1's stand?
choices: <keyframe>
<default>
<asset>
<option>
why: <keyframe> stores named poses (qpos, and ctrl too). <default> holds inherited attribute values, <asset> meshes and materials, <option> how the world behaves.

q: What happens if an MJCF file contains nothing but a <worldbody>?
choices: It compiles; the other seven sections make it a robot
It fails: <option> must be present to set a timestep
It fails: every model needs at least one actuator
It compiles but cannot step without a <keyframe>
why: A worldbody-only file compiles happily, since everything left out takes MuJoCo's defaults. "The other seven sections are the difference between a shape and a robot."

q: A <body>'s pos attribute is measured from where?
choices: From its parent body's frame
From the world origin
From the robot's centre of mass
From the nearest floor contact
why: pos is measured from the parent, not the world. That is why moving the thigh moves the shin with it, and why you never recompute a child's position by hand.

q: What is true of a <body> that contains no <joint>?
choices: It is welded to its parent and adds no freedom
It falls freely under gravity as a loose part
It can rotate about its parent but not slide
It is skipped by the compiler as having no use
why: A joint says how a body may move relative to its parent; with none, the body is welded to its parent. A free-floating body needs a <freejoint>.

q: What is a <site> in MJCF?
choices: A named point with no physics, where sensors attach
A collision shape used only under the robot's feet
A body that has mass but carries no geometry
A joint that allows no motion relative to its parent
why: A site is a named frame with no physics. Every sensor names a site; move the site in the XML and the readings change, exactly as remounting a real IMU would.

q: Why can the G1's knee never move its hand?
choices: A body moves only with the joints on its path to the root
The knee servo's gain is far too low to reach that far up the body
The hands are welded directly to the world frame
The knee and hand geoms are in different groups
why: Nesting <body> tags is the kinematic chain. The path from a hand to the pelvis passes through the waist and never through a leg, so no leg joint can move it.

q: The G1's <option> sets only integrator="implicitfast". Where do its 0.002 s timestep and its gravity come from?
choices: MuJoCo's built-in defaults
The scene file's own <option> line
The stand keyframe's values
The <default class="g1"> block
why: An MJCF is a diff against a default robot: every attribute you leave out still has a value. "A number you never wrote is shaping your results."

q: None of the G1's 29 actuator lines contains a gain. Where does k_p = 500 come from?
choices: <default class="g1">, inherited via childclass="g1" on the pelvis
MuJoCo's built-in default gain, applied to every position actuator
The stand keyframe, which stores one gain per actuator
The <option> section, next to the integrator setting
why: <default class="g1"> holds kp = 500 and the pelvis carries childclass="g1", so every tag beneath inherits it. Classes nest: foot inherits from collision, which inherits from g1.

q: What does inheritrange="1" do on the G1's position actuators?
choices: Copies each joint's range onto its actuator's control range
Copies the parent body's mass and inertia onto its child
Makes each actuator inherit k_p from its joint's stiffness
Lets ctrl exceed the joint's travel by a safety margin
why: The joint range becomes the actuator's ctrlrange, so a command outside the joint's travel cannot even be expressed.

q: The G1's group-2 geoms have contype="0" conaffinity="0". What does that mean?
choices: They are drawn but invisible to physics
They collide but are never drawn at all
They collide only with the floor plane
They carry the link's mass and inertia
why: Group 2 is the pretty mesh, excluded from collision. Group 3 holds what actually touches the world. One link is drawn one way and collided another.

q: How are the G1's 72 geoms split?
choices: 1 floor, 35 visual in group 2, 36 collision in group 3
1 floor, 36 visual in group 3, 35 collision in group 2
72 collision meshes, each drawn exactly as it collides
29 visual, 29 collision and 14 contact sites
why: 72 = 1 floor + 35 visual meshes (group 2, contype = conaffinity = 0) + 36 collision geoms (group 3). Group 2 is drawn, group 3 collides.

q: Why does each G1 foot touch the floor through small spheres rather than through its mesh?
choices: Sphere contacts are cheap and stable; mesh-on-mesh is neither
Meshes cannot carry mass or inertia inside a MuJoCo model at all
Spheres render better than meshes in the viewer
A mesh foot would need its own extra actuator
why: Choices like this keep a 29-joint humanoid fast enough to learn in. Mesh-on-mesh contact is expensive and jittery.

q: Each G1 foot touches the floor through what?
choices: Four spheres of 5 mm radius
Eight spheres of 2 mm radius
One box the size of the sole
Its STL mesh, exactly as drawn
why: Four 5 mm spheres per foot, so 8 contacts when standing. They carry friction 0.6; everything else uses MuJoCo's default 1.0.

q: In the G1's frame, which axis points to the robot's left?
choices: +y
+x
−y
+z
why: +z is up (gravity along −z), +y is the robot's left (left hip at y = +0.064 m), and +x is forward.

q: Nodding your head "yes" is a rotation about which axis, and what is it called?
choices: About y (left): pitch
About x (forward): roll
About z (up): yaw
About y (left): roll
why: Roll is about x (ear to shoulder), pitch about y (nod "yes"), yaw about z (shake "no").

q: A robot tipping over sideways is rotating about which axis?
choices: x (forward): roll
y (left): pitch
z (up): yaw
x (forward): yaw
why: Tipping sideways turns about the forward axis x, which is roll. Leaning forward or back is pitch (y); turning to face a new way is yaw (z).

q: Why does the G1 hip need three joints?
choices: Pitch to step, roll to shift weight, yaw to turn
Pitch to step, roll to turn, yaw to shift weight
Three motors are needed to share the leg's weight
One for each of the knee's three rotation axes
why: A leg does three independent things: swing forward (pitch), spread sideways and shift weight (roll), and turn (yaw). The knee needs only pitch.

q: The G1 knee's range is [−0.087, 2.880] rad. What does that tell you?
choices: It bends one way and barely straightens past zero
It bends equally far forwards and backwards from straight
It can turn through more than a full circle
It is a yaw joint with a stop at each end
why: The knee is a single pitch hinge that bends one way (up to ~165°) and stops just 5° past straight. That one-sided knee is why week 3's reachable set has a hole.

q: Which quantities belong to data rather than model?
choices: qpos, qvel, ctrl and time
body_pos and jnt_range
actuator_gainprm and body_mass
opt.timestep and opt.gravity
why: model is the robot, compiled from XML and constant while simulating (body_pos, jnt_range, actuator_gainprm, opt). data is "one robot, at one instant": qpos, qvel, ctrl, xpos, time.

q: While a simulation runs, which of the two objects changes at every step?
choices: data changes; model stays constant
model changes; data stays constant
Both change at every single step
Neither: only the viewer updates
why: model is the blueprint and does not change while you simulate; data is the moment. Confusing them is called the most common MuJoCo mistake.

q: How does week 10 run thousands of robots at once?
choices: One model serves many data
One data serves many models
Each robot recompiles its own MJCF
The model is copied into data per step
why: One description, thousands of moments: a single compiled model can drive any number of independent data objects.

q: What does mj_forward do?
choices: Computes positions from qpos without advancing time
Advances time by exactly one timestep, just like mj_step
Advances ten steps, one policy decision
Resets data back to the keyframe pose
why: mj_step advances time; mj_forward fills in positions (xpos, site_xpos) from qpos without moving the clock. That is how a pose is drawn without the robot falling over.

q: A robot has one free joint, one ball joint and twelve hinges. What are nq and nv?
why: Free 7/6, ball 4/3, hinge 1/1: nq = 7 + 4 + 12 = 23, nv = 6 + 3 + 12 = 21 (practice Q1). nq = 21 forgets both quaternions' extra number.

q: A robot has one free joint, two ball joints and six hinges. What are nq and nv?
why: nq = 7 + 2×4 + 6 = 21, nv = 6 + 2×3 + 6 = 18. 19 counts the free joint's quaternion but forgets the balls' extra numbers.

q: A fixed-base arm (no free joint) has seven hinges. What are nq and nv?
choices: nq = 7, nv = 7
nq = 8, nv = 7
nq = 7, nv = 6
why: Hinges are 1/1, and with no free joint there is no base quaternion, so nq = nv = 7. Only free and ball joints have nq > nv.

q: The week-1 two-link leg (hip and knee hinges) is wrapped in a parent body that carries a free joint. What are nq and nv?
choices: nq = 9, nv = 8
nq = 8, nv = 8
nq = 9, nv = 9
nq = 2, nv = 2
why: nq = 7 + 2 = 9, nv = 6 + 2 = 8. Without the free joint it was nq = nv = 2: bolted to the sky, able to swing but not fall.

q: The G1 is one free joint plus 29 hinges. Which line is right?
why: nq = 7 + 29 = 36, nv = 6 + 29 = 35, and 29 actuators, one per hinge.

q: Why are free and ball joints the only joints with nq > nv?
choices: A quaternion uses 4 numbers for 3 rotational freedoms
They store one extra number for the joint's own mass
Their velocity comes from an IMU, not from qvel
They are the only joint types that have limits
why: Orientation is stored as a unit quaternion (4 numbers, 1 constraint), but there are only 3 ways to turn, so qvel uses 3 angular-velocity numbers.

q: You add <freejoint/> to the upper_leg body, which already has a hip hinge. What happens?
choices: It fails, "more than 6 dofs in body"; wrap it in a parent body
It works, and nq rises by 7 while the hinge is kept exactly as it is
It works, but the compiler silently ignores the hinge
It fails, because free joints must be declared in <option>
why: A free joint is a body's entire freedom, so it cannot share a body with a hinge. The fix is a parent body that carries the free joint.

q: The G1 has 29 actuators but 35 degrees of freedom. What are the missing six?
choices: The floating base: only the floor pushes it around
Six joints locked in place by the stand keyframe
Six sensors that stand in for missing motors
The fingers, which hang passively from the wrists
why: The free joint's 6 dofs have no motor; the robot moves its base only by pushing on the floor. Fewer motors than dofs is what "underactuated" means.

q: A G1 hinge's angle sits at qpos[20]. Where is its velocity in qvel?
choices: qvel[19]
qvel[20]
qvel[21]
qvel[14]
why: The base uses 7 qpos numbers but only 6 qvel numbers, so every hinge sits one slot earlier in qvel. Look addresses up with jnt_qposadr / jnt_dofadr; never reuse one index on the other array.

q: The G1's stand keyframe has 36 numbers. What are they?
choices: 3 position + 4 quaternion + 29 joint angles
3 position + 3 rotation + 30 joint angles
6 base velocities + 30 joint angles
7 base numbers + 29 actuator torques
why: A keyframe's qpos is exactly qpos: pelvis position (3), quaternion (4), then one angle per hinge (29). <key> also sets ctrl so the servos hold the starting pose.

q: In MuJoCo, what does a base quaternion of (1, 0, 0, 0) mean?
choices: Not turned at all (scalar w first)
Turned 90° about the x axis
Turned 180° about the x axis
Invalid: its length is not equal to 1
why: u = (w, x, y, z) = (cos θ/2, n sin θ/2), scalar first. θ = 0 gives (1, 0, 0, 0), and its length is 1, so it is valid.

q: What is the MuJoCo quaternion for a 90° turn about the x axis?
why: Half the angle: θ/2 = 45°, so w = cos 45° = 0.707 and x = sin 45° = 0.707. (0, 1, 0, 0) uses the full angle (that is 180°).

q: What is the MuJoCo quaternion for a 120° turn about the z axis?
why: θ/2 = 60°: w = cos 60° = 0.5, z = sin 60° = 0.866. Using cos 120° = −0.5 forgets the half angle; (0.866, …, 0.5) is a 60° turn; the last is about x.

q: A base quaternion reads (0, 1, 0, 0). How far is the base turned?
choices: 180° about x
90° about x
0°: not turned
360° about x
why: w = cos(θ/2) = 0 means θ/2 = 90°, so θ = 180°. Reading w as the angle itself gives 90°. A quaternion holds half the angle.

q: Which of these could be a valid MuJoCo orientation quaternion?
why: It must have unit length: 0.36 + 0.64 = 1. The others give 1.64, 2 and 0.5. One constraint on four numbers leaves three freedoms.

q: How does MuJoCo's integrator update the base quaternion at each step?
choices: It turns it by angle h|ω| about the axis of ω
It adds h × ω to the four quaternion numbers
It adds h × ω to x, y, z and leaves w alone
It re-reads the orientation from the keyframe
why: qvel has 3 angular-velocity numbers and the quaternion has 4, so "quaternion + h × velocity" does not even match in size. The integrator rotates it instead, keeping it unit length.

q: A parent body sits at world (0, 0, 1), not rotated. Its child has pos="0 0 -0.4". Where is the child's origin in the world?
why: p_child = p_parent + R_parent · pos_child = (0, 0, 1) + (0, 0, −0.4) = (0, 0, 0.6). (0, 0, −0.4) treats pos as a world position.

q: A parent at world (1, 0, 0) is turned 90° about z, so its own x axis points along world +y. A child has pos="0.2 0 0". World position of the child?
why: Walk the typed offset along the parent's own axes: 0.2 along the parent's x, which now points along world +y, so (1, 0, 0) + (0, 0.2, 0). (1.2, 0, 0) ignores the rotation.

q: Why can a proportional servo holding a leg against gravity never reach its target exactly?
choices: It makes torque only by being wrong: a load needs an error
The damper k_v·q̇ cancels the spring at rest
MuJoCo adds a little random noise to every single servo's torque
The integrator loses a little energy every step
why: At rest q̇ = 0, so τ = k_p(ctrl − q) must equal gravity's torque: q − ctrl = −τ_g/k_p. "A non-zero load needs a non-zero error." At rest the damper does nothing.

q: A servo with k_p = 400 N·m/rad holds a joint against 8 N·m of gravity. What is the steady error, and what if k_p is doubled?
choices: 0.02 rad; doubling k_p halves it to 0.01 rad
0.02 rad; doubling k_p removes it entirely
3,200 rad; doubling k_p halves it
0.02 rad; doubling k_p doubles it to 0.04 rad
why: |q − ctrl| = τ_g / k_p = 8 / 400 = 0.02 rad (practice Q3). Droop ∝ 1/k_p, so doubling halves it to 0.01 rad: smaller, never zero. 3,200 multiplies instead of dividing.

q: A joint carries 30 N·m of gravity torque and its droop must be at most 0.01 rad. What is the smallest k_p that achieves this?
choices: 3,000 N·m/rad
300 N·m/rad
0.3 N·m/rad

q: What actually removes the steady-state droop of a P servo?
choices: An integral term, or gravity feedforward
Raising k_p high enough that the droop reaches zero
Raising the damping gain k_v
A smaller physics timestep
why: Raising k_p only shrinks the error (∝ 1/k_p) and never zeroes it; k_v does nothing at rest; the timestep is not the cause. A term that remembers (I) or one that knows gravity in advance (feedforward) does it (week 5).

q: The week-1 two-link leg's hip droop at k_p = 200 and at k_p = 5?
choices: −0.080 rad and −0.858 rad
−0.858 rad and −0.080 rad
−0.080 rad and exactly 0 rad
−0.008 rad and −0.080 rad
why: Measured: −0.080 rad at k_p = 200 and −0.858 rad at k_p = 5. Lower gain, more sag, and never zero at any gain.

q: Why does the droop demo command a bent pose (hip 1.2, knee −0.8) rather than ctrl = 0?
choices: Zero is a hanging leg's rest, so any gain would "succeed"
Zero is outside the hip joint's allowed range of travel
Commanding zero triggers BADQACC at every timestep
A position servo cannot be commanded to exactly zero
why: For a leg hanging down, zero is also gravity's rest position, so a k_p sweep from there shows no droop and proves nothing. A bent pose makes gravity fight the servo.

q: In M(q)·v̇ + c(q, v) = τ + τ_contact, what is c?
choices: Gravity plus Coriolis and centrifugal terms (qfrc_bias)
The floor's push and the joint-limit forces (qfrc_constraint)
The torques the actuators push with (qfrc_actuator)
The diagonal of the mass matrix, one per joint
why: c is the bias force: gravity plus the forces that come from moving. τ is the actuators, τ_contact the floor and limits, and M the 35×35 mass matrix, which changes with the pose.

q: What does one call of mj_step do, in order?
choices: Solves for the accelerations, then integrates q and v by h
Integrates q and v by h, then solves for the accelerations
Reads the sensors, then runs your policy to choose ctrl
Solves for contacts only; integration is a separate call
why: (1) Solve M v̇ + c = τ + τ_contact for v̇, then (2) integrate q and v forward by one timestep h. Your controller writes ctrl before the call.

q: Explicit Euler is first order. A run with h = 0.004 s has an error of 8 mm. Roughly what error at h = 0.001 s?
choices: 2 mm
0.5 mm
8 mm
32 mm
why: First order: error ∝ h, so a 4× smaller step gives a 4× smaller error, 2 mm. 0.5 mm would be second order (∝ h²).

q: What is MuJoCo's "Euler" integrator?
choices: Semi-implicit: velocity first, then position with the new velocity
Explicit: position and velocity both from the old values
Fully implicit: it solves a nonlinear system of equations at every step
Fourth-order Runge–Kutta with an adaptive step size
why: v_{n+1} = v_n + h·v̇_n, then q_{n+1} = q_n + h·v_{n+1}. One swapped line versus explicit Euler, and it is the difference between a spring that works and one that explodes.

q: For an undamped spring ẍ = −ω²x, how does explicit Euler behave?
choices: It grows at every h > 0: |λ| = √(1 + h²ω²) > 1
It is stable whenever h < 2/ω, like MuJoCo's
It is stable whenever h < 1/ω, half the bound
It decays slowly to zero at every h > 0
why: The step matrix has eigenvalues 1 ± ihω, of size √(1 + h²ω²) > 1 for every h > 0. It cannot hold an undamped spring at any timestep.

q: An explicit-Euler spring simulation keeps growing. A student halves h. What happens?
choices: It still grows, only more slowly
It becomes stable once h < 2/ω
It becomes exactly accurate
It grows faster than before
why: |λ| = √(1 + h²ω²) is above 1 for every h > 0, so a smaller step only slows the growth. The h < 2/ω bound belongs to semi-implicit Euler.

q: Explicit Euler on an undamped spring with hω = 0.75. By what factor does the swing grow each step?
why: |λ| = √(1 + h²ω²) = √(1 + 0.5625) = √1.5625 = 1.25. 1.5625 forgets the square root; 1.00 would be the semi-implicit eigenvalue size.

q: A spring–mass system has ω = 50 rad/s. What is the largest stable timestep for semi-implicit Euler?
why: h < 2/ω = 2/50 = 0.04 s (practice Q4). 0.02 s is 1/ω, the common slip of forgetting the 2.

q: A 4 kg mass sits on a spring of k = 10,000 N/m. Largest stable semi-implicit step?
why: ω = √(10,000/4) = √2500 = 50 rad/s, so h < 2/50 = 0.04 s. 0.02 s ignores the 4 kg (that is the 1 kg example from the guide); 0.0008 s is 2m/k with no root.

q: A servo spring is stable up to h = 0.02 s. Its stiffness is raised four times. What is the new largest stable step?
why: h < 2√(m/k): four times k doubles ω, so the bound halves to 0.01 s. Dividing by 4 (0.005 s) forgets the square root.

q: A spring is stable up to h = 0.01 s. The mass on it is made four times heavier. New largest stable step?
why: h < 2√(m/k): four times m halves ω, so the bound doubles to 0.02 s. "The stiffer the spring or the lighter the thing on it, the smaller the step."

q: Semi-implicit Euler, ω = 100 rad/s, h = 0.03 s. What happens?
choices: It explodes: hω = 3 is past the bound of 2
It is bounded: hω = 3 is still under π
It is bounded but inaccurate, just under 2
It is exact: semi-implicit has no bound
why: Stability needs |tr A| = |2 − h²ω²| ≤ 2, i.e. hω ≤ 2. Here hω = 3, tr A = −7, so one eigenvalue exceeds 1. π is the steps-per-oscillation count, not the bound on hω.

q: The bound h < 2/ω, read as samples of the spring's oscillation, says what?
choices: Take more than π ≈ 3 steps per oscillation
Take more than 2 steps per oscillation
Take at least 100 steps per oscillation
Take more than 2π ≈ 6 steps per oscillation
why: The period is 2π/ω, and h < 2/ω means period/h > π. Below about three snapshots per swing the simulation cannot see the oscillation.

q: Semi-implicit Euler at hω = 1.99 releases a spring from 1 cm. What does it do?
choices: Stays bounded but swings to about 10 cm: wrong
Matches the true 1 cm swing, being under the bound
Explodes, because it is so close to the limit of 2
Is reset to zero by BADQACC with a warning
why: Just below the bound the motion is bounded but badly wrong (3.2 cm at hω = 1.9, 10 cm at 1.99). "Stable is not the same as accurate."

q: With the damper computed at the old velocity (MuJoCo's Euler), what does ζ = 1 do to the stability bound on hω?
choices: Shrinks it from 2 to about 0.83: less stable
Raises it from 2 to about 4.83: more stable
Leaves it at 2: damping never moves the bound
Removes it: any step is stable when damped
why: Explicit damper: hω < 2(√(1 + ζ²) − ζ) = 2(√2 − 1) ≈ 0.83 at ζ = 1. An explicitly computed damper makes the stiff spring less stable, the opposite of intuition.

q: With the damper computed at the new velocity (implicitfast), ζ = 1 gives which bound on hω?
choices: About 4.83
About 0.83
Exactly 2
About 3.14
why: Implicit damper: hω < 2(√(1 + ζ²) + ζ) = 2(√2 + 1) ≈ 4.83. 0.83 is the explicit-damper (Euler) bound; 2 is the undamped bound.

q: A critically damped servo (ζ = 1) has ω = 100 rad/s. Using the explicit-damper bound hω < 0.83, what is the largest stable step under Euler?
choices: About 0.008 s
About 0.02 s
About 0.048 s
About 0.083 s
why: h < 0.83/100 ≈ 0.0083 s. 0.02 s is the undamped 2/ω; 0.048 s is the implicitfast bound 4.83/ω.

q: At h = 0.002 s the G1's stiffest servo sits at hω ≈ 0.44. What is hω at h = 0.004 s, and how does Euler fare against its ζ ≈ 1 bound of 0.83?
choices: 0.88: past 0.83, so Euler fails
0.22: well inside, Euler holds
0.88: inside 4.83, so Euler holds
1.76: past 2, both integrators fail
why: Doubling h doubles hω to 0.88 > 0.83, so plain Euler shakes the G1 to the floor at 0.004 s, while implicitfast (bound 4.83) stands. 4.83 is implicitfast's bound, not Euler's.

q: What happens to the standing G1 at h = 0.004 s under each integrator?
choices: Euler shakes it to the floor; implicitfast stands
Euler stands; implicitfast shakes it to the floor
Both stand: the bound is far away at that step
Both raise BADQACC on the very first step
why: Measured in the guide. "The integrator line in the file is a safety margin": at 500 Hz both hold, at 0.004 s only implicitfast does.

q: At dt = 0.02 s with the servos on, the two-link leg's qpos comes back as [0, 0]. What happened?
choices: BADQACC: accelerations blew up and the state was reset
The servos held the commanded pose perfectly, with no droop at all
The leg settled at gravity's rest, hanging straight
The simulation ended early because it was so fast
why: Past the stability bound MuJoCo raises mjWARN_BADQACC and resets the state to zero, which reads like success. Always check data.warning.

q: At dt = 0.02 s with the servos off, the passive swing gives different final angles but no warning at all. What is this?
choices: A silent approximation: wrong, with no warning
A silent failure: BADQACC reset the state
Correct: a passive swing ignores the timestep
A crash: the simulation stops with an error
why: Exercise 14: servos off is merely different and wrong (silent approximation); servos on blows up and resets (silent failure). Neither stops the program.

q: Why must the G1's standing contact normal forces sum to its weight?
choices: Its CoM does not accelerate, so ΣF_n − mg = 0
The servos are tuned to push down with exactly mg
MuJoCo clamps every contact force to the weight
Each of the 8 spheres carries exactly mg / 8
why: Newton vertically: m·z̈ = ΣF_n − mg, and standing still z̈ = 0. A free physics check that needs no ground truth. The 8 spheres do not share equally.

q: A standing robot's controller stiffens every servo. What happens to the sum of the contact normal forces?
choices: Nothing: motors push the robot against itself
It rises along with the larger servo torques in the legs
It falls as the legs become stiffer
It doubles while the servos saturate
why: Internal forces cannot change the total ground reaction; only acceleration of the CoM can. Standing still, ΣF_n = mg whatever the motors do.

q: A 400 N robot stands with its CoM at x = 0, heel spheres at x = −5 cm and toe spheres at x = +15 cm. How is the load split?
choices: Heels 300 N, toes 100 N
Heels 100 N, toes 300 N
Heels 200 N, toes 200 N
Heels 400 N, toes 0 N
why: Moments about the CoM balance: F_heel × 5 = F_toe × 15, so heels carry 3×: 300 N and 100 N. The nearer contact carries more; swapping them is the usual slip.

q: Standing G1: how many contacts, and how is its 327 N shared?
choices: 8 contacts; heels ~225 N, toes ~102 N
8 contacts; heels ~102 N, toes ~225 N
2 contacts; ~164 N under each sole mesh
36 contacts; one per collision geom
why: Four spheres per foot give 8 contacts summing to 327.1 N. The CoM (x = +0.3 cm) is nearer the heels (−5 cm) than the toes (+12 cm), so heels carry ~225 N.

q: Where are the G1's eight standing contacts declared in the MJCF?
choices: Nowhere: MuJoCo finds contacts every step
In <sensor>, one entry per foot sphere
In <keyframe>, together with stand
In <actuator>, as ground-reaction motors
why: Contacts are not declared; the engine detects them each step from the collision geoms, and you can read them with mj_contactForce.

q: After one mj_step from the stand keyframe, what does the pelvis do, and why?
choices: Rises 0.018 mm: the foot spheres start ~2 mm inside the floor
Drops 0.018 mm: gravity acts before the contacts form
Stays exactly still: the stand pose is perfectly balanced already
Drops 2 mm until the foot spheres first touch the floor
why: The keyframe leaves the 8 foot spheres ~2 mm inside the floor. MuJoCo's contacts are slightly soft (penetration makes force), so the floor pushes the robot up first.

q: Which describes the G1's stand keyframe?
choices: Pelvis 0.79 m, quaternion (1,0,0,0), only the arms bent
Pelvis 0.79 m, quaternion (1,0,0,0), knees bent 1.28 rad
Pelvis 0.134 m, quaternion (0,0,0,1), every joint at zero
Pelvis 0.79 m, quaternion (0,1,0,0), arms straight down
why: Pelvis at 0.79 m, not turned, elbows at 1.28 rad; every leg joint is exactly zero, a perfectly straight leg. 0.134 m is where the limp robot ends up.

q: Every leg joint in stand is exactly zero. Is a perfectly straight leg a good starting point for inverse kinematics?
choices: No: a perfectly straight leg is a singularity
Yes: zero is the most neutral possible seed
Yes: zero is gravity's own rest for the leg
No: zero is outside the knee's joint range
why: The straight leg is the worst IK seed: the Jacobian has no direction that shortens the leg. The knee range [−0.087, 2.880] does include zero.

q: How fast does the G1 simulate on one CPU core?
choices: ~15,000–16,000 steps/s, about 30× real time
~500 steps/s, exactly real time
~1,500 steps/s, about 3× faster than real time
~150 million steps/s, 300,000× real time
why: Roughly 15–16 thousand physics steps per second at 500 Hz is about 30× real time (machine dependent). Week 10 wants 150 million steps, so this number decides afternoon versus month.

q: A simulation runs 20,000 physics steps per second at a 0.002 s timestep. How many times faster than real time?
why: Each second of compute advances 20,000 × 0.002 = 40 s of robot time: 40× real time.

q: Two runs of the same G1 fall, same code, same machine. How much do their final states differ?
choices: Exactly 0.0: bit-identical
About 1e-12, round-off noise
About 1 cm, contact chaos
It varies: MuJoCo seeds randomly
why: On one machine the simulator is exactly deterministic: same input, same arithmetic, same answer, a hard zero.

q: The same limp fall ends at 0.134 m on a laptop and 0.142 m on Colab. Why?
choices: The arithmetic is reordered and the fall amplifies it
MuJoCo injects fresh random noise into each new run of a fall
Colab runs with a different default gravity
One of the two installs must be broken
why: Not randomness: different hardware reorders floating-point operations, and a falling robot amplifies tiny differences exponentially. Stable equilibria (0.792 m) reproduce exactly.

q: How should a lab test check the result of a falling robot?
choices: Assert direction and size, e.g. "dropped more than 0.5 m"
Assert the final torso height equals 0.134 m exactly
Assert the height to within 1e-6, after fixing the random seed
Assert nothing at all: falls can never be tested
why: "Never assert or grade an exact number from a fall; assert direction and size." A seed makes a run repeatable on one machine, not identical across machines.

q: To test for chaos, a student nudges the G1's base x position by 1e-12 before the fall and sees the gap stay 1×. What can they conclude?
choices: Nothing: a shift on a flat floor is a symmetry; nudge a joint
The fall is not chaotic, since the nudge did not grow at all in 3 s
MuJoCo ignores any perturbation smaller than 1e-9
The fall is chaotic only in the vertical z direction
why: Translating along an infinite flat floor is an exact symmetry: the same trajectory, shifted. Test sensitivity along a direction that is not a symmetry, such as a knee angle (grows ~10⁵× in 3 s).

q: The gap between two runs grows as δ ≈ δ₀·e^{λt}, here a factor of 10 every second. If δ₀ = 1e-9 rad, what is δ after 3 s?
choices: 1e-6 rad
3e-9 rad
1e-8 rad
1e-12 rad
why: ×10 per second for 3 s is ×1000: 1e-9 × 10³ = 1e-6. 3e-9 treats the growth as linear; 1e-8 counts only one second.

q: What growth rate was measured for the falling G1's run-to-run gap?
choices: λ ≈ 3.7/s: about ×40 per second, ~10⁵ in 3 s
λ ≈ 0.37/s: about ×1.4 per second, ~3 in 3 s
λ ≈ 37/s: about ×10¹⁶ per second, overflow
λ = 0: runs are bit-identical, so no growth
why: A 10⁻¹² rad knee nudge grows about 10⁵-fold in 3 s, λ ≈ 3.7/s. λ = 0 confuses determinism (same input, same output) with insensitivity (nearby inputs stay nearby).

q: What question does forward kinematics (FK) answer?
choices: Given the joint angles, where is the foot?
Given a desired foot position, which joint angles reach it?
Given the joint torques, how will the robot accelerate?
Given the foot contacts, where is the centre of pressure?
why: FK goes angles → foot. Foot → angles is inverse kinematics (week 3); torques → accelerations is dynamics.

q: Why does a real robot need forward kinematics at all?
choices: Encoders report only joint angles; no sensor reports the foot position
Encoders report foot positions, but only in the pelvis frame
Its IMU drifts, so FK must integrate the accelerometer into a position
Its servos accept only foot positions, so angles must be converted first
why: Six leg encoders give six angles and no position. FK is the function that turns those angles into 'the foot is here'.

q: In MuJoCo, what does an x prefix on an array (xpos, site_xpos, xmat) tell you?
choices: Computed by mj_forward, in world coordinates
Declared in the MJCF, relative to the parent body
Measured along the body's own x axis only
Stored as a homogeneous 4-vector with a trailing 1
why: The naming rule: x = computed, world frame; no x = declared in the model, relative to the parent (body_pos vs xpos, site_pos vs site_xpos).

q: In week 2's terms, what is mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)?
choices: MuJoCo's own forward kinematics: qpos in, every x quantity out
One 2 ms physics step that integrates qvel into qpos and time
A converter that turns the qpos quaternion into Euler angles
A solver that finds qpos from a desired foot position
why: mj_forward IS forward kinematics, which is why you can write your own FK and demand agreement to the last decimal. Stepping time is mj_step.

q: Complete the professor's line: "Most robotics bugs are …"
choices: one number used in the wrong frame
a sign error inside a rotation matrix
an off-by-one in a joint index
a quaternion read scalar-last
why: The others are real bugs too, but the quoted line is about frames: a position is only true in a stated frame, and wrong-frame bugs look like a robot that is slightly, confusingly wrong.

q: At stand, the same left foot is at z = 0.033 in the world frame, z = −0.757 in the pelvis frame and z = −0.654 relative to the hip. Which statement is right?
choices: All three are correct, each in its own stated frame
Only the world value is a position; the others are offsets
Only the pelvis value is right, because the robot measures from its body
None are usable until mj_forward converts them to one frame
why: A frame is an origin plus three axes, and a position is true only relative to one. Same physical point, three legitimate answers, none usable without its label.

q: A robot's pelvis stands upright (R = I) at height 0.80 m. Its foot site is at world z = 0.03 m. What is the foot's z in the pelvis frame?
why: p_pelvis = Rᵀ(p_world − t) = 0.03 − 0.80 = −0.77 m: the foot is below the pelvis. Adding the height (0.83) instead of subtracting is the usual slip.

q: What are the three columns of a rotation matrix R?
choices: Where the x, y and z axes land after the rotation
Where the axes came from before the rotation
The rotation axis scaled by cos θ, sin θ and 1
The roll, pitch and yaw angles as unit vectors
why: R = [R e_x | R e_y | R e_z]: column 1 is where x ends up, and so on. 'Where they came from' would be the rows (the inverse, Rᵀ).

q: Rotate the vector (2, 1, 0) by Rz(90°). Result?
Which matrix is Ry(90°), written as rows?
why: Ry(θ) = [[c,0,s],[0,1,0],[−s,0,c]]: the minus is bottom-left. The 'tidied' version with the minus top-right is Ry(−90°).

q: Rotate (1, 0, 0) by Ry(90°). Result?
why: Column 1 of Ry(90°) is (c, 0, −s) = (0, 0, −1): x dips down. With +y pointing away from you, a positive turn about y looks clockwise in the xz view.

q: A student 'fixes' Ry(θ) by moving its minus sign to the top-right corner so it looks like Rx and Rz. What has she actually written?
choices: Ry(−θ): every positive pitch now swings the leg forward
The same Ry(θ): the sign position is only a convention
A mirror with det = −1 that is no longer a rotation
A matrix that is now wrong only in its bottom (z) row
why: [[c,0,−s],[0,1,0],[s,0,c]] is exactly Ry(−θ), still a rotation (det +1). Ry's minus sign looks misplaced and is not; moving it flips the sense of every pitch.

q: A link of length 0.4 m hangs from a pivot to (0, 0, −0.4). It is turned by Ry(90°). Where is its tip, as (x, z)?
why: tip = (−L sin θ, −L cos θ) = (−0.4, 0): horizontal and behind the pivot. A positive pitch swings the leg backwards, not forwards.

q: The same 0.4 m hanging link is turned by Ry(30°). Where is its tip, as (x, z)?
why: x = −0.4 sin 30° = −0.20 and z = −0.4 cos 30° ≈ −0.35. Swapping sin and cos, or dropping the minus on x, are the usual slips.

q: On the G1, which way does a positive hip pitch swing the leg, and what follows?
choices: Backwards, so the week-4 crouch commands hip pitch −0.35
Forwards, so the week-4 crouch commands hip pitch +0.35
Toward +y, so the left leg crouch uses hip roll −0.35
Backwards, so the week-4 crouch commands knee −0.70
why: Ry's signs make positive pitch swing the leg back, so a knee-forward crouch needs negative hip pitch. The crouch is (−0.35, 0, 0, +0.70, −0.35, 0): the knee is positive.

q: What do R_ab and t_ab describe?
choices: Frame b as seen from a: they take b-coordinates into a-coordinates
Frame a as seen from b: they take a-coordinates into b-coordinates
The turn from a to b, applied after the shift from b to a
The difference between the two frames' world positions
why: Subscripts read right to left: R_ab p_b turns a point written in b into a's coordinates. The inner letters (b, b) match and cancel, leaving a.

q: Which expression is wrong on sight, from the subscripts alone?
choices: R_ab p_a
R_ab p_b
R_ab R_bc
T_ab T_bc p_c
why: In a valid product the inner letters match and cancel (ab·b, ab·bc). R_ab expects a point written in b, so feeding it p_a is a frame bug.

q: In p_a = R_ab p_b + t_ab, what is t_ab?
choices: Where frame b's origin sits, in a's coordinates
Where frame a's origin sits, in b's coordinates
The point p after it has been turned into frame a
The scalar distance between the two frames' origins
why: t_ab is the arrow from a's origin to b's origin, written along a's axes. Adding it turns 'an arrow from b's origin' into 'an arrow from a's origin'.

q: Frame b is turned by R_ab = Rz(90°) and its origin is at t_ab = (2, 0, 0). A point is at p_b = (1, 0, 0). What is p_a?
why: Turn, then shift: Rz(90°)(1, 0, 0) = (0, 1, 0), plus (2, 0, 0) gives (2, 1, 0). Shifting first and then turning gives (0, 3, 0); forgetting R gives (3, 0, 0).

q: Practice Q5: write t_ac in terms of R_ab, t_ab and t_bc.
choices: t_ac = R_ab t_bc + t_ab
t_ac = t_ab + t_bc
t_ac = R_ab t_ab + t_bc
t_ac = R_ab (t_ab + t_bc)
why: Substitute p_b = R_bc p_c + t_bc into p_a = R_ab p_b + t_ab: the shift part is R_ab t_bc + t_ab. The parent's rotation acts on the child's offset; plain addition forgets it.

q: R_ab = Rz(90°), t_ab = (1, 0, 0), t_bc = (2, 0, 0). What is t_ac?
why: t_ac = R_ab t_bc + t_ab = (0, 2, 0) + (1, 0, 0) = (1, 2, 0). (3, 0, 0) forgets to turn the child's offset; (2, 1, 0) turns the wrong offset.

q: What is R_ac when chaining a ← b ← c?
choices: R_ab R_bc
R_bc R_ab
R_abᵀ R_bc
R_ab + R_bc
why: p_a = R_ab(R_bc p_c + t_bc) + t_ab, so the rotation part is R_ab R_bc. The subscripts confirm it: the inner b's cancel.

q: A student's FK loop writes pos = pos + body_pos[b] instead of pos = pos + rot @ body_pos[b]. What happens?
choices: Child offsets are added unturned: the leg swings from the wrong place
Nothing on the G1, because every G1 joint has jnt_pos = 0
Only the foot's orientation is wrong; its position is still correct
A constant 2 µm error appears, just like the paper model's
why: "The parent's rotation acts on the child's offset. Forget it and the leg swings from the wrong place." The jnt_pos = 0 fact is about the anchor term, a different line.

q: In a 4×4 homogeneous transform, why is a 1 appended to a point?
choices: So the multiplication picks up the translation column
So the bottom row keeps the 4×4 matrix invertible
To mark the point as having been normalised to unit length
So the rotation block is applied once per frame
why: T p̃ = [R p + t·1; 1]: the appended 1 multiplies t. A direction gets a 0 instead, so it turns but does not shift.

q: T has R = I and t = (5, 0, 0). Apply it to the direction (1, 0, 0, 0) and to the point (1, 0, 0, 1). Results (first three numbers)?
choices: Direction (1, 0, 0); point (6, 0, 0)
Direction (6, 0, 0); point (6, 0, 0)
Direction (1, 0, 0); point (1, 0, 0)
Direction (5, 0, 0); point (6, 0, 0)
why: A direction's 0 ignores the translation column, so it is unchanged; the point's 1 picks up t. Directions turn but do not shift.

q: Code transforms a joint axis (a direction) with a 1 appended, like a point. What goes wrong?
choices: The translation gets added, so the axis is shifted like a point
Nothing: the fourth component is ignored for unit vectors
The axis is turned twice by R and comes out reversed
The result has five components and the multiply raises
why: Directions get a 0 so they turn without shifting. With a 1, the axis is moved by t and is no longer a direction at all.

q: With homogeneous transforms, how is a six-joint leg written?
choices: T1 T2 ⋯ T6, read left to right from root to tip
T1 + T2 + ⋯ + T6, one term per link
T6 T5 ⋯ T1, read from the foot up to the pelvis
The six rotation blocks multiplied, translations added after
why: Chaining is plain multiplication, root on the left. The 4×4 product does the 'multiply rotations, turn-and-add translations' bookkeeping automatically.

q: p_a = R p_b + t with R = Rz(90°) and t = (1, 0, 0). Given p_a = (1, 1, 0), what is p_b?
why: p_b = Rᵀ(p_a − t) = Rᵀ(0, 1, 0) = (1, 0, 0). Using R instead of Rᵀ gives (−1, 0, 0); turning before subtracting (Rᵀp_a − t) gives (0, −1, 0).

q: Why is the inverse transform p_b = Rᵀ(p_a − t) and not a general matrix inverse?
choices: A rotation's columns are perpendicular unit vectors, so R⁻¹ = Rᵀ
For a rotation t is always zero, so only R needs undoing
Every rotation matrix is symmetric, so Rᵀ = R = R⁻¹ always
3×3 matrices have no general inverse, only a transpose
why: RRᵀ = I is the defining property of a rotation, so one transpose replaces a general inversion. Rotations are not symmetric in general (Rᵀ is the reverse turn).

q: Turn (1, 0, 0) by Rz(90°) first, then by Rx(90°): compute Rx(90°) Rz(90°) (1, 0, 0). Result?
why: Rz(90°) sends x to (0, 1, 0); Rx(90°) then sends that to (0, 0, 1). The other order, Rz Rx (1, 0, 0), gives (0, 1, 0): matrix products do not commute.

q: my_fk writes rot = rot @ Rj, with the joint on the right. Why?
choices: The joint turns about the link's own, already-moved axis
Products of rotations commute, so either side gives the same answer
On the left it would turn about the link's own axis instead
The right side is where world-axis rotations are applied
why: Read a product left to right, root to tip: each factor acts in the frame its left neighbours produced. Rj on the left would turn about a world axis, building a different machine.

q: A teammate says "roll 10°, pitch 20°, yaw 5°" fully specifies the foot's orientation. What is missing?
choices: The order (convention) in which the three turns are applied
Nothing: three angles always fix a rotation uniquely
The units, since MuJoCo expects every angle in radians
The quaternion sign, since q and −q are different
why: Turning a book about vertical then tipping it differs from the reverse. Three angles mean nothing until the order is stated, which is why the chain composes matrices instead.

q: In the paper leg, the ankle uses sin(θ1 + θ2) and cos(θ1 + θ2). Why do the angles add?
choices: The knee angle is measured from the thigh, which has already turned by θ1
Because sin θ1 + sin θ2 equals sin(θ1 + θ2) for small enough angles
The knee angle is measured from vertical, so θ1 must be added back
The knee motor is mounted on the pelvis, next to the hip pitch motor
why: Each dashed 'zero' line follows the previous link, so the shin's direction is θ1 + θ2 from vertical. That is chaining rotations, in 2-D.

q: Paper leg: hip at z = 0.8, L1 = 0.35, L2 = 0.30, θ1 = 90°, θ2 = −90°. Where is the ankle (x, z)?
Paper leg: hip at z = 1, L1 = 0.4, L2 = 0.3, θ1 = −30°, θ2 = +60°. What is the ankle's x?
why: knee_x = −0.4 sin(−30°) = +0.20; ankle_x = 0.20 − 0.3 sin(30°) = 0.05. Using θ2 alone (sin 60°) gives about −0.06; flipping the sign gives −0.05 or +0.35.

q: The crouch is hip −0.35, knee +0.70, ankle −0.35. Why does the foot stay level?
choices: The three pitch angles sum to zero
The knee angle is exactly twice the hip angle
The hip and knee angles have opposite signs
The ankle roll is held at zero
why: Pitch angles add down the chain, so the foot's pitch is −0.35 + 0.70 − 0.35 = 0. A foot that lands tilted trips.

q: How closely does the paper two-link model match MuJoCo's foot, and why not better?
choices: About 2 µm, a constant offset, because it is a model of the leg
About 10⁻¹⁶ m, because it is the same floating-point computation
About 2 mm, random noise from the contact solver
About 4 mm, because it uses the true 3-D thigh length
why: The flat model reaches ~2 µm and the residual is constant (at the zero pose the foot sits 2.3 µm behind the hip). The full 3-D chain reaches 10⁻¹⁶.

q: Composing the full 3-D chain body by body, how well does your FK match site_xpos?
choices: About 10⁻¹⁶ m: machine precision
About 2 µm: same as the paper model
About 1 mm: limited by the meshes
About 10⁻⁸ m: limited by ε = √u
why: The 3-D chain is the same computation MuJoCo does, so it agrees to ~10⁻¹⁶, a hundred million times tighter than the paper model's 2 µm.

q: Which thigh length does the planar (x, z) formula need?
choices: 0.3366 m, the in-plane projection
0.3409 m, the true 3-D length
0.3000 m, the same as the shin
0.6409 m, the thigh plus the shin
why: The hip→knee vector splays 5.4 cm sideways, so a flat picture needs its xz projection, 0.3366 m. The true 0.3409 m is what week 3's law of cosines uses; both are correct for their job.

q: On the G1 leg, which set of lengths is right?
choices: Shin 0.3000 m; ankle to foot site 0.0176 m
Shin 0.3366 m; ankle to foot site 0.0350 m
Shin 0.3409 m; ankle to foot site 0.0176 m
Shin 0.3000 m; ankle to foot site 0.0540 m
why: Shin 0.3000 m, ankle-pitch anchor to the foot site 0.0176 m. 0.035 m is the site's height above the contact spheres; 0.054 m is the thigh's sideways splay.

q: Where is the left_foot site?
choices: At the ankle-roll link origin, 3.5 cm above the contact spheres
On the sole, at the centre of the four 5 mm contact spheres
At the toe tip, about 12 cm ahead of the ankle-roll axis
At the ankle-pitch joint, 1.76 cm above the foot's sole
why: The left_foot site is not the sole. FK reports where that frame is; touching the ground is a separate question (at stand the site reads z = 0.033 while the sole is on the floor).

q: A crouch figure keeps the pelvis at standing height and shows the foot 3.7 cm above the floor. Diagnosis?
choices: Correct: kinematics places a pose; it does not settle a robot
A bug: the FK loop forgot to rotate the knee's offset
A bug: the foot site is being drawn 3.5 cm too high
Correct only because gravity was switched off in the model
why: Bending the knee with the pelvis held shortens the leg, so the foot rises. Nothing is simulated in FK; gravity never enters. It must be annotated, not 'fixed'.

q: Two week-2 gaps: how far is the crouched foot off the floor (pelvis pinned), and how high is the foot site above the contact spheres?
choices: 3.7 cm off the floor; site 3.5 cm above the spheres
3.5 cm off the floor; site 3.7 cm above the spheres
11.1 cm off the floor; site 1.76 cm above the spheres
0 cm off the floor; site 3.5 cm above the spheres
why: Bending one knee with the pelvis held lifts the foot 3.7 cm (week 2b's symmetric squat: 11.1 cm). Separately, the left_foot site sits 3.5 cm above the spheres even when standing.

q: Which pairing of representation and job is right?
choices: Euler angles: saying a rotation out loud
Quaternion: reading a rotation at a glance
Axis-angle: composing many rotations
Rotation matrix: compact storage
why: Matrix: acting on vectors, composing. Quaternion: storing, interpolating (bad at reading). Axis-angle: angular velocity and error (bad at composing). Euler: saying out loud (gimbal lock).

q: Numbers and constraints: which row is right?
choices: Matrix 9 / 6; quaternion 4 / 1; axis-angle 3 / 0; Euler 3 / 0
Matrix 9 / 3; quaternion 4 / 1; axis-angle 3 / 0; Euler 3 / 0
Matrix 9 / 6; quaternion 4 / 0; axis-angle 3 / 1; Euler 3 / 0
Matrix 9 / 6; quaternion 4 / 1; axis-angle 3 / 0; Euler 3 / 1
why: All have 3 freedoms: 9 − 6 = 4 − 1 = 3 − 0 = 3. The matrix's 6 rules are unit columns (3) and perpendicular columns (3); the quaternion's one is ‖q‖ = 1.

q: All four rotation representations have 3 freedoms. What does the guide say makes them behave differently?
choices: Their constraint count (6, 1, 0, 0)
Their number count (9, 4, 3, 3)
Whether they are in degrees or radians
Whether MuJoCo can convert them to R
why: "The constraint count is the reason they differ": six rules to keep true drift; one is easy to restore (q /= ‖q‖); zero means any numbers are valid.

q: Why does qpos store the floating base's orientation as 4 numbers rather than 9?
choices: A quaternion has one constraint to keep true, a matrix has six
A rotation has four freedoms, one more than a position
Euler angles need a fourth number to fix their order
The fourth number stores the pelvis height above the floor
why: A matrix you keep composing drifts off SO(3) and needs re-orthonormalising against six rules; a quaternion needs only q /= norm(q).

q: A 3×3 matrix R is a rotation if and only if…
choices: RRᵀ = I and det R = +1
RRᵀ = I, with no further condition
det R = +1, with no further condition
every entry lies between −1 and +1
why: RRᵀ = I gives orthonormal columns; det = +1 excludes mirrors. det = −1 with RRᵀ = I is a reflection: a mirrored robot, not a turned one.

q: M = diag(1, −1, 1) satisfies MMᵀ = I. Is it a rotation?
choices: No: det M = −1, so it is a mirror
Yes: MMᵀ = I is all a rotation needs
Yes: it is a 180° turn about the y axis
No: a rotation cannot have a negative entry
why: det = 1·(−1)·1 = −1, a reflection (the left↔right mirror of week 2b). A 180° turn about y is diag(−1, 1, −1), with det +1.

q: What does Rodrigues' formula R = I cos θ + (1 − cos θ) uuᵀ + [u]× sin θ require of u?
choices: It must be a unit vector
It must be one of the coordinate axes
It must be perpendicular to the vector being turned
It must have a positive z component
why: The derivation splits v into parts along and across a unit axis; the code normalises u first. Any direction works once normalised.

q: Rodrigues is fed the axis (1, 1, 1) without normalising it, with θ = 120°. What comes out?
choices: A matrix that is not a rotation (RRᵀ ≠ I)
The same rotation, since only the axis direction matters
The same axis with the angle scaled by √3
An error raised by the formula
why: uuᵀ and [u]× scale with |u| and |u|², so the pieces no longer combine into an orthonormal matrix. Nothing raises: the formula silently returns garbage.

q: Rodrigues with u = (0, 0, 1) and θ = 180°: what is R?
choices: I
why: cos θ = −1, sin θ = 0: R = −I + 2uuᵀ = diag(−1, −1, 1). x and y reverse, z stays. diag(−1, −1, −1) has det −1, a reflection.

q: What is the MuJoCo quaternion (w, x, y, z) for a 180° turn about z?
why: q = (cos θ/2, n sin θ/2) = (cos 90°, 0, 0, sin 90°) = (0, 0, 0, 1). Using the full angle gives (−1, 0, 0, 0), which is the identity; (0.707, 0, 0, 0.707) is only 90°.

q: What is the MuJoCo quaternion (w, x, y, z) for a 90° turn about z?
why: Half angle: (cos 45°, 0, 0, sin 45°). Plugging in the full 90° gives (0, 0, 0, 1), which is a 180° turn. (0.5, 0, 0, 0.5) is not even unit length.

q: Turn 120° about the unit axis (1, 1, 1)/√3. What is the quaternion (w, x, y, z)?
choices: (½, ½, ½, ½)
(−½, ½, ½, ½)
why: w = cos 60° = ½; each vector part = sin 60°/√3 = (√3/2)/√3 = ½. The full-angle slip gives cos 120° = −½; (0.866, …) is a 60° turn.

q: The 120° turn about (1, 1, 1)/√3 is the permutation matrix [[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,1,0]]. Apply it to (1, 2, 3).
why: Rv = (z, x, y): row 1 copies z, row 2 copies x, row 3 copies y. That is the x → y → z → x cycle as arithmetic.

q: Why do q and −q give exactly the same rotation matrix?
choices: Every entry of R is quadratic in (w, x, y, z), so the signs cancel
MuJoCo normalises every quaternion so that w is positive
−q is the inverse rotation, and the inverse has the same R
Only w appears squared in R, so its sign cancels out
why: Each term of the quaternion→R formula has two factors, so flipping all four signs changes nothing. (The inverse would be (w, −x, −y, −z), a different R.)

q: Practice Q6: two foot quaternions have every component different. Can you conclude the feet are oriented differently?
choices: No: one could be the negative of the other, the same rotation
Yes: unit quaternions map one-to-one onto rotations
Yes, provided both have been normalised to unit length
No, but only because floating-point rounding blurs them
why: q and −q are the same rotation (and conventions differ: scalar first vs last), so never compare orientations number by number.

q: MuJoCo stores (w, x, y, z). What happens if your code reads it as scalar-last (x, y, z, w), as SciPy and ROS do?
choices: Silently wrong but legal: a 7.6° tilt reads as 174.8°
A ValueError, since the quaternion stops being unit length
The inverse rotation, which shows up clearly as a sign flip
A small error only, since w is close to 1 for small tilts
why: A reordered unit quaternion is still unit length and legal, so nothing raises; the foot simply turns upside down. That plausibility is what makes the bug nasty.

q: Which quaternion convention does MuJoCo use?
choices: (w, x, y, z): scalar first
(x, y, z, w): scalar last, like SciPy
(w, x, y, z): scalar first, like ROS
(x, y, z, w): scalar last, like qpos[3:7]
why: MuJoCo is scalar first (qpos[3:7] = w, x, y, z). SciPy and ROS are scalar last, which is why mixing libraries flips feet.

q: MuJoCo's lowercase 'xyz' Euler sequence means…
choices: Intrinsic: R = Rx(roll) Ry(pitch) Rz(yaw)
Extrinsic: R = Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll)
Intrinsic: R = Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll)
Extrinsic: R = Rx(roll) Ry(pitch) Rz(yaw)
why: Lowercase 'xyz' is intrinsic and composes left to right, Rx Ry Rz. Uppercase 'XYZ' (extrinsic) equals Rz Ry Rx. The order of the product is the convention.

q: Euler 'xyz' with roll 90°, pitch 90°, yaw 0: R = Rx(90°) Ry(90°). Where does R send (1, 0, 0)?
why: Ry(90°)(1, 0, 0) = (0, 0, −1); Rx(90°)(0, 0, −1) = (0, 1, 0). Same as the 120° turn: x → y. Multiplying in the reversed order, Ry Rx, gives (0, 0, −1).

q: Euler 'xyz' with pitch at exactly 90°: what happens to roll and yaw?
choices: They stop being independent; only their sum survives
They swap roles but both stay fully independent
Both are forced to zero by the conversion
Only their difference survives, not their sum
why: At pitch 90°, (roll 30, yaw 0), (0, 30), (15, 15) and (45, −15) give a bit-identical quaternion: one knob does nothing. That is gimbal lock.

q: Pitch is exactly 90° (Euler 'xyz'). Which (roll, yaw) gives the same rotation as roll 40°, yaw 10°?
choices: Roll 25°, yaw 25°
Roll 40°, yaw −10°
Roll 30°, yaw 30°
Roll 30°, yaw −20°
why: At pitch 90° only roll + yaw survives: 40 + 10 = 50 = 25 + 25. The others sum to 30, 60 and 10.

q: How quickly does gimbal lock fade as pitch moves away from 90°?
choices: Slowly: swapped roll/yaw differ by 0.5° at pitch 89° and 5° at 80°
Instantly: at 89° the two angles are fully independent again
Not at all: below 90° the degeneracy stays identical
Linearly: exactly 1° of separation per degree from 90°
why: It is not a knife edge: near 90° one knob does almost nothing. This is why we never hand a controller three Euler angles.

q: "Compress to store, expand to act, compress again to correct." Which form does the acting?
choices: The rotation matrix
The quaternion
The axis-angle vector
The Euler triple

why: Mirror of the left is −0.100220; the difference from −0.100210 is 0.000010 m = 10 µm, one part in ten thousand.

q: Mirrored hand positions agree only to about 10⁻⁵ m, not 10⁻¹⁶. Diagnosis?
choices: A 10 µm asymmetry in the MJCF itself, not a bug
A bug in mirror(): pitch must be negated as well
Floating-point round-off growing along the arm
A quaternion read scalar-last somewhere in the arm
why: The shoulder body_pos values differ by 10 µm. Do not 'fix' the mirror code chasing it, and never assert 1e-16 near it.

q: set_pose bends both legs into a squat and the feet end 0.111 m off the floor. Diagnosis?
choices: Correct: set_pose pins the pelvis, so bent legs are shorter
A bug: set_pose forgot to call mj_forward afterwards
A bug: the squat angles were applied in degrees
