Correct only because the servos were switched off
why: Kinematics places a pose; it does not settle a robot. A real squat lowers the pelvis by about that amount, which IK and the walker decide.

q: What does soc4180.set_pose do besides writing your angles?
choices: Resets to stand first (unless reset=None), then calls mj_forward
Steps physics until the robot settles onto the floor
Lowers the pelvis so the feet stay on the floor
Copies the angles into ctrl for the servos to track
why: Each pose is then a complete description, not something accumulated from earlier calls, and the x quantities are ready when it returns. It never lowers the pelvis.

q: With the pelvis pinned by set_pose, how far does a symmetric squat lift the feet?
why: 0.111 m for the 2b squat (hip −0.6, knee 1.2, ankle −0.6). 0.037 m is week 2's single-leg crouch; 0.035 m is the foot site's height above the spheres.

q: Why write set_pose(model, data, left_elbow=1.2) rather than data.qpos[25] = 1.2?
choices: Ids move when the MJCF changes, names do not; wrong slots never raise
qpos[25] raises an IndexError on the G1, whose arm starts at 26
Indexing qpos by slot is far slower than a name lookup
qpos[25] is read in degrees, while set_pose takes radians
why: Write names, not slots. qpos[25] is the left elbow today, but the one bug you cannot catch by reading is a valid index that means the wrong joint.

q: You want to measure how the torso moves. Which point should you track?
choices: The imu_in_torso site, not the torso_link origin
The torso_link body origin, the centre of the torso
The pelvis IMU, which sees everything mounted above it
The head, which is welded rigidly to the torso
why: torso_link's origin lies on the waist axes and barely moves (0.4 mm under waist_yaw, 0 under roll and pitch); the IMU site moves 4/15/15 mm.

q: Forward kinematics always gives exactly one foot position. What can inverse kinematics give for a foot target?
choices: None, two, infinitely many, or an exploding one
Always exactly one solution, just like forward kinematics
Always exactly two solutions: knee forward or knee back
At most one solution, because the leg is a single serial chain
why: IK reverses FK and the question misbehaves: out of reach gives none, the knee gives two, extra joints give infinitely many, and near a singularity the answer explodes. Only FK is guaranteed one answer.

q: When does an IK problem have infinitely many solutions?
choices: When the leg has more joints than foot constraints
When the target lies outside the reachable annulus
When the knee is bent exactly 90 degrees
When the Jacobian is square and has full rank
why: Extra joints leave freedom over: a whole family of joint vectors puts the foot in the same place. Outside the annulus there are none, and a square full-rank Jacobian gives a unique local step.

q: A pose that IK solves with zero error is placed on the simulated robot under gravity. What does the course say can happen?
choices: It may still fall over: IK is geometry, not balance
It cannot fall, because the IK residual is zero
It falls only if the damping λ was set too small
It falls only if the target was outside the annulus
why: IK only places a pose; whether the robot can hold it depends on where its weight is, which IK never checks. A perfectly solved pose can be one the robot cannot hold for a moment.

q: Closed-form IK for a 6-joint foot pose is possible. Why does the course use differential IK instead?
choices: Robot-specific, brittle to model changes, hard to add limits to
No closed-form solution exists for any leg with more than two joints
Closed form needs thousands of iterations, so it is too slow for 500 Hz
Closed form only works when the leg is perfectly straight
why: The derivation exists but is tied to one robot, breaks when the model changes, and is hard to extend with joint limits or obstacles. The tempting claim that no closed form exists is false: the guide says it can be solved.

q: In MuJoCo's convention (the one the course uses), what knee angle θ is a perfectly straight leg?
why: The G1's knee counts from zero when the leg is straight. The 180° answer is the triangle's interior corner, which is π − θ, not the joint angle.

q: With θ the knee joint angle (0 = straight), which formula gives it from the hip-to-foot distance d?
choices: cos θ = (d² − ℓ1² − ℓ2²) / (2ℓ1ℓ2)
cos θ = (ℓ1² + ℓ2² − d²) / (2ℓ1ℓ2)
cos θ = (d² − ℓ1² − ℓ2²) / (ℓ1 + ℓ2)
cos θ = (ℓ1² + d² − ℓ2²) / (2ℓ1d)
why: For the joint angle the sign is flipped relative to the textbook interior-angle law, since the interior corner is π − θ and cos(π − θ) = −cos θ. The last formula is the hip corner φ, not the knee.

q: Two-link leg, ℓ1 = 0.3 m, ℓ2 = 0.4 m, target at d = 0.5 m. What is the knee angle θ (0 = straight)?
why: d² = 0.25 = 0.09 + 0.16, so the numerator d² − ℓ1² − ℓ2² is 0 and cos θ = 0, θ = 90°. Whenever d² = ℓ1² + ℓ2² the knee is a right angle.

q: Two-link leg, ℓ1 = 0.4 m, ℓ2 = 0.2 m, target at d = 0.6 m. What is the knee angle θ (0 = straight)?
choices: 0°: the leg is straight
180°: the leg is folded
90°: a right angle
60°: an equilateral bend
why: d = ℓ1 + ℓ2 is full reach: cos θ = (0.36 − 0.16 − 0.04)/(0.16) = 1, so θ = 0. Answering 180° confuses the joint angle with the triangle's interior corner.

q: Two-link leg, ℓ1 = 0.5 m, ℓ2 = 0.3 m, target at d = 0.2 m. What is the knee angle θ (0 = straight)?
choices: 180°: folded completely back
0°: perfectly straight at full reach
90°: a right angle at the knee
None: the target is unreachable
why: cos θ = (0.04 − 0.25 − 0.09)/0.30 = −1, so θ = 180°. d = |ℓ1 − ℓ2| is the inner edge of the annulus: just reachable, with the shin folded onto the thigh.

q: Two-link leg, ℓ1 = ℓ2 = 1 m, target at d = 1 m. What is the knee angle θ (0 = straight)?
why: cos θ = (1 − 1 − 1)/2 = −0.5, so θ = 120°. 60° is the interior corner of the equilateral triangle (π − θ), the sign slip the formula is written to avoid.

q: arccos returns one knee angle θ for a reachable target. What is the second solution?
choices: −θ: the knee bent the other way
π − θ: the interior corner of the triangle
θ + π: the same leg pointing backwards
None: arccos is one-to-one, so θ is unique
why: cos(−θ) = cos θ, so the mirror-image knee also satisfies the law of cosines: knee forward and knee back. π − θ is the triangle's interior angle, not a second joint solution.

q: A two-link leg has ℓ1 = 0.5 m and ℓ2 = 0.3 m. Is a target 0.1 m from the hip reachable?
choices: No: the reachable set starts at |0.5 − 0.3| = 0.2 m
Yes: every target closer than 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8 m is reachable
Yes: close targets are easier, the knee just bends more
No: the reachable set starts at the shin length, 0.3 m
why: Reach is an annulus |ℓ1 − ℓ2| ≤ d ≤ ℓ1 + ℓ2, here 0.2 to 0.8 m, and 0.1 m is inside the hole. Forgetting the inner radius is the classic slip.

q: A two-link leg has ℓ1 = 0.4 m and ℓ2 = 0.3 m. Which hip-to-foot distances can it reach?
choices: From 0.1 m to 0.7 m
From 0 m to 0.7 m
From 0.3 m to 0.7 m
From 0.1 m to 0.5 m
why: Inner radius |0.4 − 0.3| = 0.1 m, outer 0.4 + 0.3 = 0.7 m. 0 to 0.7 m forgets the inner radius; 0.5 m is √(ℓ1² + ℓ2²), the right-angle knee, not the edge.

q: A two-link leg has equal links, ℓ1 = ℓ2 = 0.35 m. Which hip-to-foot distances can it reach?
choices: Any distance from 0 to 0.70 m: no hole
Only from 0.35 m to 0.70 m: never closer than one link
Only exactly 0.70 m, at full stretch
From 0.35 m to 0.49 m, the right-angle reach
why: |ℓ1 − ℓ2| = 0 when the links are equal, so the annulus becomes a full disc and the foot can even fold back onto the hip. Unequal links are what create the hole.

q: A foot target sits 2 cm from the G1's hip. Why can the IK not reach it?
choices: It is inside the annulus hole, under 0.0409 m
It can: a closer target is always easier, the knee simply bends more
Because the Jacobian cannot be computed so close to the hip joint
Because the damping λ switches off every direction near the hip
why: Too close is as impossible as too far: the G1 thigh (0.3409 m) and shin (0.3000 m) cannot fold to less than 0.0409 m. The belief that closer is always easier ignores the inner radius.

q: What is the reachable hip-to-foot range of the G1's two-link leg model?
why: Thigh 0.3409 m and shin 0.3000 m give |ℓ1 − ℓ2| = 0.0409 and ℓ1 + ℓ2 = 0.6409. 0.70 m is a distance the lab measured as unreachable.

q: The lab tabulated the G1 knee angle against hip-to-foot distance. Which row matches?
why: A short distance needs a deep bend and the knee straightens toward full reach (0.6409 m). The 174° row is the old bug that reported the interior corner instead of the joint angle.

q: Which pair of hip-to-foot distances did the lab find unreachable for the G1 leg?
why: 0.02 m is inside the 0.0409 m hole and 0.70 m is beyond the 0.6409 m outer edge. The other distances all lie in the annulus.

q: The knee's sensitivity is |dθ/dd| = d / (ℓ1ℓ2 sin θ). What happens as the leg straightens (θ → 0)?
choices: It diverges, because sin θ → 0 in the denominator
It goes to zero, because the knee stops moving
It stays constant at about 1/ℓ1 rad per metre
It is largest at θ = 90°, then falls toward zero
why: sin θ → 0 at full reach, so the knee angle needed per metre of target blows up. That is the two-link picture of the singularity.

q: Near full reach, what does one millimetre of change in the foot target ask of the knee?
choices: Whole degrees of knee motion
A thousandth of a degree, almost nothing
Exactly one milliradian per millimetre
No motion, since the knee is already locked
why: Because |dθ/dd| diverges as sin θ → 0, a tiny change in d near the straight leg demands a large change in θ: "one millimetre asks for degrees of knee".

q: Same leg, nearly straight in both cases (d ≈ ℓ1 + ℓ2). Compare |dθ/dd| at sin θ = 0.01 with sin θ = 0.1.
choices: About 10 times larger at sin θ = 0.01
About 10 times smaller at sin θ = 0.01
About 100 times larger at sin θ = 0.01
The same, since d hardly changes
why: |dθ/dd| = d/(ℓ1ℓ2 sin θ) with d nearly fixed, so dividing sin θ by 10 multiplies the sensitivity by 10 (1/sin θ, not 1/sin² θ).

q: What equation does differential IK solve at each iteration?
choices: J Δq = e: a small joint change, then repeat
J q = x: the joint angles for the target in one shot
Δq = J e: the error multiplied by the Jacobian
e = J⁻¹ x: the foot error from the foot position
why: Differential IK does not solve for the angles; it solves for a small change Δq that moves the foot by e, then repeats. J maps joint motion to foot motion, so it multiplies Δq, not e.

q: With J = UΣVᵀ, what does the plain inverse Δq = J⁻¹e do to each foot direction?
choices: Divides it by its own singular value σᵢ
Multiplies it by its own singular value σᵢ
Divides every direction by σ_max
Divides it by σᵢ² + λ²
why: J⁻¹ = VΣ⁻¹Uᵀ, so the component of e along uᵢ is scaled by 1/σᵢ. A direction the leg barely moves (tiny σᵢ) needs an enormous joint motion.

q: A foot request of 0.05 m lies along a direction with singular value σ = 0.1 m/rad. How much joint motion does the plain inverse ask?
choices: 0.5 rad
5 rad
0.05 rad
why: Plain inverse divides by σ: 0.05/0.1 = 0.5 rad. Multiplying instead (0.005 rad) is the slip of applying J instead of J⁻¹.

q: The same 0.05 m request now lies along a direction with σ = 10⁻⁶ m/rad. What does the plain inverse ask?
choices: About 50,000 rad
About 5 × 10⁻⁸ rad
About 0.05 rad
About 500 rad
why: 0.05/10⁻⁶ = 5 × 10⁴ rad. That is the straight-leg story: the algebra returns an exact but absurd answer.

q: Lowering the G1 foot 5 cm with the plain inverse: what does it cost crouched (σ_min 0.089) and at stand (σ_min 9e-7)?
choices: 0.56 rad crouched, about 55,000 rad at stand
About 55,000 rad crouched, 0.56 rad at stand
0.56 rad in both poses: the request is the same
0.04 rad crouched, 0.56 rad at stand
why: Same request, different σ_min: crouched it is half a radian shared by hip, knee and ankle; straight it is tens of thousands of radians. 0.04 rad is what DLS with λ = 10⁻³ gives at stand.

q: At stand the plain inverse returns Δq ≈ 55,000 rad and the residual ‖JΔq − e‖ is exactly zero. What should you conclude?
choices: The algebra succeeded and commanded the impossible
The step is exact, so the robot can execute it
The zero residual proves the target is reachable
λ should be lowered further to keep it exact
why: A zero residual only says the linear equation is satisfied; it says nothing about whether the joint motion is sane. Near a singularity the exact answer is enormous.

q: An IK step reports a residual of 0 to machine precision. Can you conclude the joint motion is sensible?
choices: No: check ‖Δq‖ too; near a singularity exact steps are huge
Yes: a zero residual is the definition of a perfect IK solution
Yes, as long as the Jacobian is square (six joints, six constraints)
No, because a zero residual always means the target was unreachable
why: A zero residual does not mean a sensible solution: the plain inverse at stand is exact and asks for ~55,000 rad. Squareness only makes J⁻¹ defined, not well behaved.

q: In SVD terms, what is the singularity at the G1's stand pose?
choices: σ_min ≈ 0: the Jacobian has (almost) lost a rank
σ_max → ∞: the Jacobian entries blow up
All singular values equal 1: J is a rotation
All singular values are equal: κ = 1
why: A singularity is a pose where J loses a rank, σ_min ≈ 0 (9e-7 at stand, a rank gone up to round-off). The entries of J stay finite; it is the smallest gain that vanishes.

q: Which cost does damped least squares minimise?
choices: ‖JΔq − e‖² + λ²‖Δq‖²
‖JΔq − e‖² − λ²‖Δq‖²
‖Δq‖² + λ²‖e‖²
‖JΔq − e‖ + λ‖e‖²
why: Error left over plus joint motion spent, weighted by λ². A minus sign would reward big motion; penalising ‖e‖ makes no sense since e is given, not chosen.

q: Setting the gradient of the DLS cost to zero gives which update?
choices: Δq = (JᵀJ + λ²I)⁻¹ Jᵀ e
Δq = (JᵀJ − λ²I)⁻¹ Jᵀ e
Δq = (JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹ Jᵀ e
Δq = Jᵀ (JᵀJ + λ²I)⁻¹ e
why: The normal equations are (JᵀJ + λ²I)Δq = Jᵀe. The other forms either flip the damping sign or put the matrices in an order whose sizes do not match.

q: Why does the DLS inverse always exist for λ > 0, even at a singularity?
choices: JᵀJ + λ²I is positive definite for any λ > 0
Because J itself is always invertible once λ is added to it
Because λ cancels the zero singular values exactly
Because the identity is invertible, any sum with it is invertible
why: ‖Jv‖² ≥ 0 and λ²‖v‖² > 0 for v ≠ 0, so the matrix is positive definite and invertible. The last option is false in general: I + (−I) is not invertible.

q: How are (JᵀJ + λ²I)⁻¹Jᵀe and Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹e related?
choices: The same vector, by the push-through identity
They differ; the second is the more accurate one
They agree only when λ = 0, the plain inverse
They agree only when J is square (6 × 6)
why: Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I) = (JᵀJ + λ²I)Jᵀ, so the two expressions are equal for any J and any λ > 0. They differ only in the size of the matrix inverted.

q: J is 6 × 12 (six foot constraints, twelve joints). Which DLS form is the cheaper solve?
choices: Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹e, since it inverts a 6 × 6 matrix
(JᵀJ + λ²I)⁻¹Jᵀe, since it inverts a 6 × 6 matrix
Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹e, since it inverts a 12 × 12 matrix
Neither: both forms invert a 12 × 12 matrix
why: JJᵀ is 6 × 6 and JᵀJ is 12 × 12. With more joints than constraints the right-hand form inverts the smaller matrix; for one G1 leg (6 × 6) they cost the same.

q: With J = UΣVᵀ, DLS scales direction i by σᵢ/(σᵢ² + λ²). What does that do?
choices: σᵢ ≫ λ gets the true inverse 1/σᵢ; σᵢ ≪ λ is switched off
σᵢ ≫ λ is switched off; σᵢ ≪ λ gets the true inverse 1/σᵢ
Every direction is scaled down by the same factor λ
Every direction gets 1/σᵢ, plus a constant λ²
why: For σᵢ ≫ λ the gain ≈ 1/σᵢ; for σᵢ ≪ λ it ≈ σᵢ/λ² → 0. λ is a threshold: weak directions are ignored rather than amplified.

q: What does raising the damping λ trade?
choices: Accuracy for stability
Stability for accuracy
Speed for memory
Reach for joint limits
why: A larger λ keeps steps small near singularities (stable) but delivers less of the requested motion per step (less accurate). It cannot change what the leg can reach.

q: DLS gain σ/(σ² + λ²) with σ = 1 and λ = 0.1. About how large is it?
choices: ≈ 0.99, almost the true inverse 1/σ = 1
≈ 0.10, the direction is switched off
≈ 9.9, amplified about tenfold
≈ 0.01, which is just λ²
why: 1/(1 + 0.01) ≈ 0.99. Since σ ≫ λ, DLS behaves like the plain inverse here.

q: DLS gain σ/(σ² + λ²) with σ = 0.001 and λ = 0.1. About how large is it?
choices: ≈ 0.1, nearly switched off
≈ 1000, the plain inverse 1/σ
≈ 0.001, equal to σ
≈ 10, equal to 1/λ
why: σ ≪ λ, so the gain ≈ σ/λ² = 0.001/0.01 = 0.1, against 1000 for the plain inverse. The weak direction is suppressed instead of amplified.

q: DLS gain σ/(σ² + λ²) when σ = λ = 0.1. What is it?
choices: 5, half the plain inverse's 10
10, the plain inverse 1/σ
0.05, half of σ
50, five times the plain inverse
why: 0.1/(0.01 + 0.01) = 5, while 1/σ = 10. At σ = λ the gain is exactly 1/(2λ): the crossover between "true inverse" and "switched off".

q: With λ = 0.01, what is the largest gain σ/(σ² + λ²) any direction can receive?
choices: 50, reached at σ = λ
100, which is 1/λ
10,000, which is 1/λ²
Unbounded as σ → 0
why: The gain peaks at σ = λ with value 1/(2λ) = 50, and falls to 0 for smaller σ. "Unbounded" describes the plain inverse 1/σ, which DLS exists to avoid.

q: At stand the weak direction has σ ≈ 9 × 10⁻⁷. With λ = 10⁻³, about how much joint motion does a 5 cm request along it cost?
choices: About 0.04 rad
About 55,000 rad
About 50 rad
Exactly 0 rad
why: σ ≪ λ so the gain ≈ σ/λ² = 9e-7/1e-6 = 0.9, and 0.05 × 0.9 ≈ 0.045 rad (the guide's 0.04 rad). 55,000 rad is the undamped plain inverse.

q: DLS from the straight-leg stand pose keeps the step small, yet the foot still does not go down. Why?
choices: Damping cannot invent a direction the pose lacks
λ is still too small; a larger λ would deliver the full 5 cm
λ is too large; λ → 0 would deliver the full 5 cm safely
The solver needs more iterations to accumulate the motion
why: At a straight leg no joint motion shortens it (σ_min ≈ 9e-7). Larger λ switches that direction off; smaller λ asks for absurd motion. No λ creates the missing direction.

q: IK must lower the pelvis but starts from the straight-leg stand keyframe and barely moves. What is the fix?
choices: Start from a crouched seed instead
Raise λ until the step converges
Lower λ to recover the exact inverse
Raise the iteration count tenfold
why: The fix for a straight leg is a different starting pose, not a different λ or more iterations. That is why every gait in the course starts crouched, and why humans do not walk with locked knees.

q: IK from a straight leg leaves a residual of 0.79 after 40 iterations and exactly 0.79 after 400. Should you raise λ, raise the iterations, or change the seed?
choices: Change the seed to a crouch: the missing direction is geometry
Raise the iterations: 400 was still not enough to converge
Raise λ: the damping is too weak to stabilise the solve
Lower λ: the damping is hiding the true exact solution
why: A residual that ignores the iteration count is geometry, and damping cannot add the missing direction. From a crouched seed the same request reaches 2.2e-6.

q: A tracking residual stays at 2.68e-3 m whether you run 12, 40 or 120 iterations. What kind of problem is this?
choices: A geometry problem: the target is out of reach
A solver problem: it needs even more iterations
A damping problem: λ is set far too high
A precision problem: double precision ran out
why: A residual that does not shrink with more iterations is geometry (unreachable target). Only a residual that shrinks slowly is a solver problem.

q: When is a large IK residual a solver problem rather than a geometry problem?
choices: When it shrinks slowly as iterations are added
When it stays exactly the same however many iterations
Whenever it is larger than one millimetre
Whenever the Jacobian is non-square
why: A slowly shrinking residual means the solver is getting there and needs more effort. A residual frozen regardless of iterations means the target itself is unreachable.

q: How does the course say you should check whether a foot target is reachable?
choices: With a ruler: distance against the annulus
Run the solver for many more iterations and watch
Lower λ until the residual reaches zero
Check whether the condition number is below 20
why: Reachability is a property of the target, not of the solver. You can check it before running anything by measuring the distance against |ℓ1 − ℓ2| ≤ d ≤ ℓ1 + ℓ2.

q: A 90-target circle tracked with warm starts, then the same circle stretched 2 cm taller. What were the worst errors?
choices: 8.4e-5 m, then 2.68e-3 m at 12, 40 and 120 iterations alike
8.4e-5 m, then 2.68e-3 m at 12 iterations, 8.4e-5 m at 120
2.68e-3 m, then 8.4e-5 m once warm starting was on
2.2e-6 m, then 0.79 m at 12, 40 and 120 iterations alike
why: The taller circle leaves the reachable set at the bottom, so its error is identical at any iteration count. 2.2e-6 and 0.79 are the crouch-vs-straight seed residuals, a different experiment.

q: What is the condition number κ = σ_max/σ_min of the leg Jacobian, geometrically?
choices: The aspect ratio of the ellipsoid J maps unit joint motions onto
The volume of the ellipsoid J maps the unit sphere of joint motions onto
The number of joints minus the number of foot constraints
The largest joint angle divided by the smallest joint angle
why: J sends every unit joint motion to a foot motion; the image is an ellipsoid with semi-axes σᵢ, and κ is its longest-to-shortest ratio. The volume would be the product of the σᵢ, not the ratio.

q: A Jacobian has σ_max = 2 and σ_min = 0.002. What is κ and roughly how many significant digits can its inverse lose?
choices: κ = 1000, about 3 digits
κ = 1000, about 1000 digits
κ = 0.001, about 3 digits
κ = 100, about 2 digits
why: κ = 2/0.002 = 1000 and log10 κ = 3 digits lost, not κ digits. 0.001 is the ratio upside down; κ is always at least 1.

q: A Jacobian has σ_max = 0.5 and σ_min = 0.05. Relative errors in e can be amplified by up to how much in Δq?
choices: 10 times (about 1 digit lost)
0.1 times (errors shrink)
100 times (about 2 digits)
0.025 times (σ_max × σ_min)
why: κ = 0.5/0.05 = 10, so ‖δΔq‖/‖Δq‖ ≤ 10 ‖δe‖/‖e‖ and log10 10 = 1 digit lost. κ ≥ 1 always, so errors are never shrunk by it.

q: κ = 1000 and the foot request e is known to 0.1 %. In the worst case, how large can the relative error in Δq = J⁻¹e be?
choices: About 100 %
About 0.1 %
About 0.0001 %
About 3 %
why: Relative error is amplified by up to κ: 1000 × 0.1 % = 100 %, i.e. the answer can be wrong by its own size. 3 % confuses κ with the digits lost (log10 κ = 3).

q: What condition numbers did the course measure for the G1 leg Jacobian?
choices: Crouch κ ≈ 20 (1 digit lost); stand κ ≈ 2×10⁶ (6 digits lost)
Crouch κ ≈ 2×10⁶ (6 digits lost); stand κ ≈ 20 (1 digit lost)
Crouch κ ≈ 1 (no digits lost); stand κ ≈ 20 (1 digit lost)
Both poses κ ≈ 20: only λ differs between them
why: The crouch ellipse is squashed about 20:1; at the straight leg it has collapsed toward a line, κ ≈ 2×10⁶. log10 κ gives 1 and 6 digits.

q: At a perfectly straight leg, what happens to the ellipse the Jacobian draws?
choices: It collapses to a line: no direction shortens the leg
It becomes a circle: every direction is equally easy
It grows without bound: every direction is amplified
It rotates 90°: up and down swap with forward and back
why: The axis that would shorten the leg is ~10⁻⁶ long. Turning any joint a little swings the foot along an arc, never toward the hip.

q: Which joint combination is the G1 leg's weakest singular direction?
choices: −0.38 hip pitch + 0.81 knee − 0.44 ankle pitch
Pure hip roll, with every other joint held still
+0.81 hip yaw − 0.44 hip roll + 0.38 ankle roll
Equal parts of all six joints, 0.41 each
why: Bend the knee and pitch hip and ankle back so the foot stays level: the one motion that shortens the leg. It moves the foot straight up or down (pure z).

q: How does the weak direction differ between the crouch and the straight stand pose?
choices: Same joint mix in both; only its gain changes, 9e-7 to 0.089
Different joint mix in each; the gain is 0.089 in both
It involves only the knee at stand, only the hip when crouched
It exists only when crouched and vanishes at stand
why: The mix −0.38/+0.81/−0.44 is the same; bending the knee restores its gain by a factor of ~100,000. At stand it still exists as a direction, it just buys almost no foot motion.

q: By roughly what factor does bending the knee from stand to the crouch raise σ_min of the leg Jacobian?
choices: About 20 (the crouch's κ)
About 2 million (stand's κ)
why: 0.089 / 9e-7 ≈ 10⁵. 20 and 2×10⁶ are the condition numbers, not the ratio of σ_min between the poses.

q: Lower the pelvis 8 cm with both feet held, 40 iterations. What residuals did the two seeds leave?
choices: Straight-leg seed 0.79; crouched seed 2.2e-6
Straight-leg seed 2.2e-6; crouched seed 0.79
Straight-leg seed 2.68e-3; crouched seed 8.4e-5
Both about 2.2e-6 once λ was tuned
why: Same request, same solver, different seed: the straight leg cannot be lowered, the crouch is solved almost exactly. 2.68e-3 and 8.4e-5 belong to the circle demo.

q: What is warm starting in IK, and what does it buy along a path?
choices: Seed each solve from the last answer: faster, and no knee flipping
Seed each solve from the crouch: slower, but always the same pose
Raise λ for the first iterations, then lower it to zero
Solve each target twice and average the two answers
why: Starting from the previous answer converges in fewer iterations and picks the solution near the last one, so the leg does not jump between knee-forward and knee-back.

q: Along a path, every IK solve is re-seeded from the same fixed pose instead of the previous answer. What can go wrong?
choices: The leg can flip between knee-forward and knee-back mid-path
Nothing: re-seeding from a fixed pose is just warm starting
The residual drops to zero, so joint motion becomes absurd
The damping λ is reset, so every step becomes singular
why: Without warm starting each solve may land on either of the two knee solutions, giving jumps in the joint trajectory. Warm starting picks the solution near the last one.

q: Why does the solver clamp joint limits after every iteration?
choices: Otherwise IK returns a pose the stops forbid
Clamping is what makes JᵀJ + λ²I invertible
Clamping replaces damping, so λ can be set to zero
Clamping is what keeps the robot from falling over
why: IK cheerfully returns a mathematically perfect pose with a joint beyond its stop unless the limits are enforced inside the loop. Clamping has nothing to do with invertibility or balance.

q: The week 3 lab game blends IK poses under real physics. What is its lesson?
choices: Every pose solves frozen; under gravity half of them fall over
Every pose IK solves can be held, since the residual is zero
Poses fall only when the IK target was out of reach
Poses fall only when λ was too small during the solve
why: IK guarantees geometry, not balance. Under gravity, half the perfectly solved poses topple; the fix is balance-aware posing and ordering.

q: In the lab game, raising both arms at once makes the G1 fall on its face. What works?
choices: One arm, then the other: order is part of the answer
A smaller λ, so the IK puts the arms up more precisely
More IK iterations, so the final pose is solved exactly
Nothing: hands-up is unreachable, so the problem has no solution
why: The final pose is fine; the route to it is what fails. "Kinematics places a pose; it does not balance a robot. The order of the poses is part of the answer."

q: Complete the professor's line: "Kinematics places a pose; it does not …"
choices: … balance a robot.
… solve the whole robot.
… need a Jacobian.
… repeat itself.
why: IK answers where the joints go, not whether the robot stays up. Balance is the business of weeks 4 and 5.

q: Why does every gait in the course start from a crouch rather than the stand keyframe?
choices: At stand the straight leg is singular: no joint motion lowers the foot
A crouch lowers the CoM height and makes ω smaller, so it falls slower
The stand keyframe violates the G1's knee joint limits
The crouch has a smaller condition number, so λ can be zero
why: Stand has every leg joint at zero, σ_min ≈ 9e-7; the crouch restores it to 0.089. (A lower CoM actually makes ω = √(g/z_c) larger, not smaller.)

q: The G1 has nv = 35 and nu = 29. What do the six missing motors correspond to?
choices: The floating pelvis: no motor to the world
The two ankles, which are passive springs
The six arm joints that are left unpowered
The quaternion's extra numbers stored in qpos
why: 35 − 29 = 6 freedoms with no motor: exactly the pelvis's free joint. The quaternion explains nq = 36 vs nv = 35, a different count.

q: A robot has one free joint and 12 hinges, and a motor on every hinge. How many of its freedoms have no motor?
why: nv = 6 + 12 = 18 and nu = 12, so 6 are unactuated: the free joint's three translations and three rotations. 7 is the free joint's qpos count (quaternion), not its freedoms.

q: Why can't the G1's 29 motors, on their own, move the robot as a whole?
choices: Internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs
They are position servos, and a position servo cannot produce any force
They are too slow, at 500 Hz, to move the whole robot's mass
They can, but only while both feet are off the ground
why: Every motor pushes one link against another inside the robot; summed over the body, those pairs cancel. Only an external force, the floor's, changes the CoM's motion.

q: Summing F = ma over every link, which equation is left for the centre of mass c?
choices: m c̈ = f_floor + m g
m c̈ = Σ motor forces + m g
m c̈ = f_floor − Σ motor forces
m c̈ = m g only
why: Internal motor forces cancel in pairs, leaving only the floor's contact force and gravity. That is why the floor is the only thing that can move the body horizontally.

q: Which statement about moving the G1's body horizontally is correct?
choices: Only the floor; motors just change how it pushes
The hip motors push the CoM forward directly, as hard as they like
Gravity alone moves it, since gravity is the only external force
The free joint carries a motor that moves the pelvis forward
why: m c̈ = f_floor + m g: gravity is purely vertical, motors are internal. The robot can only move its legs so that the floor pushes the body where it wants.

q: A foot stands on the floor. Which force can the floor exert on it?
choices: A push only, where the foot touches, within friction
A push or a pull, whichever the ankle servo commands
Any force at all, as long as the foot is flat on the ground
A downward pull whenever the robot starts to lean too far
why: The floor can push, never pull, only where a foot touches it, and sideways only as hard as friction allows. These rules are what make the CoP stay inside the support polygon.

q: How does the course describe walking?
choices: Deliberately falling and catching yourself
Holding the CoM still while the legs move
Pushing the body forward with the hip motors
Keeping the CoM over a foot at every instant
why: Lean so gravity carries the body forward, let the stance foot's force steer it, then put the next foot where it catches the fall. Keeping the CoM over a foot at all times is static walking.

q: Which describes static walking?
choices: CoM over each foot before the other lifts; slow but stable frozen
CoM between the feet, falling toward the next one; fast, and frozen it falls
CoM held at the midline the whole time; both feet always on the ground
CoM swinging outside both feet; stable only at high speed
why: Static walking keeps the robot balanced at every instant by parking the CoM over the stance foot. The second option is dynamic walking.

q: A dynamically walking robot is frozen mid-step. What happens?
choices: It falls: its CoM is between the feet, over no foot
It stays up: the ZMP plan was inside the polygon
It stays up as long as the servos hold the pose
It falls only if double support was removed
why: Dynamic walking spends most of its time with the CoM over no foot, falling toward the next one. It is fast and efficient precisely because it uses the fall; frozen, nothing catches it.

q: What is the centre of pressure (CoP)?
choices: The force-weighted mean of the contact points
The plain, unweighted average of the contact points
The point directly below the centre of mass
The contact point carrying the largest force
why: p = Σ fᵢxᵢ / Σ fᵢ: many small upward forces act like one force of size Σ fᵢ at p. It is below the CoM only when the robot is not accelerating horizontally.

q: Two contacts: 300 N at x = 0 and 100 N at x = 0.2 m. Where is the CoP?
why: p = (300·0 + 100·0.2)/400 = 0.05 m, pulled toward the heavier contact. 0.10 m is the unweighted midpoint; 0.15 m swaps the weights.

q: Three contacts: 100 N at x = 0, 100 N at x = 0.1 m, 200 N at x = 0.2 m. Where is the CoP?
why: Σfx = 0 + 10 + 40 = 50 N·m over Σf = 400 N gives 0.125 m. 0.100 m is the unweighted mean of the three positions.

q: Feet at y = −0.12 m and y = +0.12 m. All weight is on the right foot (y = −0.12), the left carries 0 N. Where is the CoP?
choices: y = −0.12 m, at the loaded foot
y = 0, at the midline
y = −0.06 m, halfway
y = +0.12 m, at the unloaded foot
why: With weight 1 on one contact and 0 on the other, the weighted average is that contact. The midline answer ignores the forces.

q: Can the CoP leave the convex hull of the contact points if one contact pushes very hard?
choices: No: non-negative weights summing to 1 keep it inside
Yes: a large enough force drags the CoP beyond that contact point
Yes, but only in single support, when there are fewer contacts
No, but only because the controller clips it back inside
why: However big one force gets, its weight approaches 1 and the CoP approaches that contact, never past it. Leaving the hull would need a negative weight: a floor that pulls.

q: What is the zero moment point (ZMP)?
choices: Where gravity plus inertia give no tipping moment
The point on the floor directly below the centre of mass
The point where the ankle servo torque is exactly zero
The floor point where the vertical contact force is zero
why: It is defined by zero moment about horizontal axes from gravity plus the body's inertia. It is below the CoM only when the CoM is not accelerating.

q: How are the ZMP and the CoP related on flat ground?
choices: The same point, computed from motion or from forces
The ZMP is always ahead of the CoP by the step length
The CoP is the ZMP projected onto the support polygon
They coincide only when the robot is standing still
why: On flat ground ZMP = CoP: the ZMP comes from the motion, the CoP from the contact forces. That is what lets the walker measure its ZMP from MuJoCo's contact forces.

q: What is the balance rule for flat feet?
choices: The ZMP must be inside the support polygon
The CoM must be inside the support polygon
The capture point must be at the midline
The ZMP must be outside the stance foot
why: A motion that needs the ZMP outside the polygon cannot happen with flat feet. The CoM itself may be outside (dynamic walking); it is the ZMP that is constrained.

q: A planned motion would need the ZMP outside the support polygon. What happens with flat feet?
choices: The foot rolls on its edge; no ankle torque stops it
The ZMP moves outside and the robot balances anyway
The floor pulls down on the heel to keep the foot flat
Friction holds the foot flat as long as μ > 0.2
why: The ZMP cannot leave the polygon, since the floor only pushes. If the motion needs it outside, the foot tips about its edge instead.

q: What is the support polygon in single support and in double support?
choices: One foot's outline; the convex hull of both feet
Both feet's outline; the stance foot only
A circle under the CoM; the line joining both ankles
The stance foot's heel; the two toes only
why: Support polygon = convex hull of the contact points. In single support that is one small foot; in double support the hull around both feet.

q: How big is one G1 foot's support polygon?
choices: About 17 × 6 cm
About 30 × 12 cm
About 10 × 10 cm
About 24 × 4 cm
why: Four contact spheres at x ∈ {−0.05, +0.12} m and y ≈ ±0.025 to 0.03 m: 17 cm by about 6 cm, to balance a 33.3 kg robot.

q: Which assumptions define the linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM)?
choices: Point mass at the CoM, massless leg to p, constant CoM height z_c
Rigid body with full inertia, massless feet, constant leg length
Point mass at the CoM, massive legs, CoM height that bobs freely
Two point masses, one per leg, joined by a spring at the hip
why: All mass in one point, a massless leg from it to the floor at p, and constant height. Constant height is what makes the model linear; a constant leg length would give the ordinary nonlinear pendulum.

q: In the LIPM derivation, what does constant CoM height give?
choices: f_z = m g: the vertical floor force equals the weight
f_x = m g: the horizontal force equals the weight
f_z = 0: the floor carries no vertical force
ẍ = 0: the CoM cannot accelerate horizontally
why: Constant height means z̈ = 0, so Newton vertically gives f_z − m g = 0. The horizontal force is what drives ẍ.

q: Why must the floor force point along the massless leg, so that f_x/f_z = (x − p)/z_c?
choices: A massless leg cannot carry a moment
Friction is zero, so only normal forces act
The servos hold the leg at a fixed angle
Gravity acts along the leg's direction
why: A massless link transmitting a moment would get infinite angular acceleration, so the force runs along it, from p to the mass. Its components are then in the ratio of the leg's sides.

q: LIPM with m = 30 kg, g = 10 m/s², z_c = 0.6 m, and the CoM 0.06 m ahead of the ZMP. What is the horizontal floor force?
choices: 3 N
why: f_x = m g (x − p)/z_c = 300 × 0.06/0.6 = 30 N. 300 N is the vertical force; 18 N forgets to divide by z_c.

q: What is the LIPM's equation of motion for the CoM's horizontal position x?
choices: ẍ = ω²(x − p), with ω = √(g/z_c)
ẍ = −ω²(x − p), with ω = √(g/z_c)
ẍ = ω²(x − p), with ω = g/z_c
ẍ = ω(x − p), with ω = √(z_c/g)
why: m ẍ = m g (x − p)/z_c. The minus sign would make it a spring (a valley); ω = g/z_c forgets the root and has the wrong units.

q: The LIPM is ẍ = ω²(x − p). Which picture fits it?
choices: A hill: it accelerates away from p, more when further
A valley: the CoM is pulled back toward p and settles there
A spring: the CoM oscillates about p at frequency ω
A ramp: the CoM accelerates at a constant g regardless of x
why: The acceleration has the same sign as x − p, so any offset grows: an inverted pendulum. Reading it as a spring is the sign error the professor warns about.

q: Why is the ZMP called the "zero moment" point in the LIPM?
choices: m z_c ẍ = m g (x − p) says the net moment about p is zero
The ankle servo applies zero torque at the stance foot
The CoM has zero angular momentum about the hip
Gravity's moment about the CoM is always zero
why: Multiply m ẍ = m g (x − p)/z_c by z_c: gravity's moment about p equals the inertial force's moment. It is an equation of motion from a moment balance, not a torque.

q: What are the units of ω = √(g/z_c)?
choices: m/s
s
m/s²
why: g/z_c is (m/s²)/m = 1/s², so ω is in 1/s and 1/ω is a time.

q: LIPM with ω = 5 /s and the CoM 0.04 m ahead of the ZMP. What is ẍ?
choices: 1 m/s², away from the ZMP
1 m/s², toward the ZMP
0.2 m/s², away from the ZMP
25 m/s², away from the ZMP
why: ẍ = ω²(x − p) = 25 × 0.04 = 1 m/s², with the sign of x − p: away. 0.2 forgets to square ω; "toward" is the valley misconception.

q: A LIPM has z_c = 0.4 m (take g = 10 m/s²). What are ω and the time constant 1/ω?
choices: ω = 5 /s, time constant 0.2 s
ω = 25 /s, time constant 0.04 s
ω = 0.2 /s, time constant 5 s
ω = 5 /s, time constant 5 s
why: ω = √(10/0.4) = √25 = 5 /s and 1/ω = 0.2 s. 25 forgets the square root; 0.2 /s inverts the ratio.

q: A robot's CoM height is multiplied by four. What happens to ω?
choices: It halves
It quarters
It doubles
It is unchanged
why: ω = √(g/z_c) ∝ 1/√z_c, and 1/√4 = 1/2. "Quarters" forgets the square root. A taller robot falls more slowly.

q: On a world with g = 1.6 m/s² and z_c = 0.4 m, what are ω and the time constant?
choices: ω = 2 /s, time constant 0.5 s
ω = 4 /s, time constant 0.25 s
ω = 0.5 /s, time constant 2 s
ω = 5 /s, time constant 0.2 s
why: √(1.6/0.4) = √4 = 2 /s, so 1/ω = 0.5 s: weaker gravity, slower fall. 5 /s is the Earth value for this height.

q: For the G1's LIPM with z_c = 0.60 m, what are ω and the time constant?
choices: ω = 4.04 /s, time constant 0.247 s
ω = 16.4 /s, time constant 0.061 s
ω = 1.64 /s, time constant 0.61 s
ω = 4.04 /s, time constant 0.65 s
why: √(9.81/0.6) = 4.04 /s, 1/ω = 0.247 s. 1.64 /s is the Moon value; 0.65 s is the step duration, not the time constant.

q: With p fixed, x(0) = x0 and ẋ(0) = v0, what is the LIPM solution?
choices: x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωt + (v0/ω) sinh ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cos ωt + (v0/ω) sin ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωt + v0 ω sinh ωt
x(t) = p + (x0 − p) sinh ωt + (v0/ω) cosh ωt
why: Trying e^(rt) gives r = ±ω, and the two initial conditions fix the cosh and sinh coefficients. cos/sin would be the spring (valley) solution; v0·ω has the wrong units.

q: How does the walking controller compute the LIPM CoM trajectory at 500 Hz?
choices: It evaluates the cosh/sinh closed form directly
It integrates ẍ = ω²(x − p) numerically with small steps
It looks the trajectory up in a table learned from data
It runs MuJoCo forward to predict where the CoM will go
why: The LIPM has an exact solution, so the controller just evaluates it at time sT. No numerical integration is needed anywhere.

q: In the LIPM, the CoM is released at rest exactly above the ZMP (x0 = p, v0 = 0). What happens?
choices: It stays put, but any offset would grow
It slides toward the nearer foot and stops there
It oscillates about p with period 2π/ω
It falls forward at once with acceleration g
why: x(t) = p for all t: an equilibrium, but on top of a hill. Any offset x0 − p grows like cosh ωt.

q: Released at rest with the CoM 2 cm from p, after a time where cosh ωt ≈ 7, how far is it from p?
choices: About 14 cm
About 2 cm
About 0.3 cm
About 9 cm
why: With v0 = 0, x − p = (x0 − p) cosh ωt = 0.02 × 7 = 0.14 m. The error multiplies; it does not add (9 cm would be 2 + 7).

q: A step lasts 0.6 s and ω = 5 /s. How many time constants long is the step?
why: 1/ω = 0.2 s, and 0.6/0.2 = 3 (= ωT). 0.12 is T/ω and 8.3 is ω/T, both upside down; 15 multiplies by ω².

q: With z_c = 0.6 m, a 0.65 s step is 2.6 time constants. By roughly how much does a starting error grow in one step?
choices: About ×7 (cosh 2.6)
About ×2.6 (one per τ)
About ×13 (e^2.6)
why: Released at rest, the distance from p grows like cosh ωT, and cosh 2.6 ≈ 7. 2.6 is the number of time constants, not the growth; e^2.6 ≈ 13 forgets that cosh is half of e^ωT plus a vanishing term.

q: A starting error grows about ×7 over each 0.65 s step. What does the professor conclude?
choices: That is why a walker must act every step
So errors average out if you take many steps
So longer steps let the error settle down
So the LIPM is of no use for real walking
why: Errors multiply, never settle: left alone for a step or two, any mistake is ×7, ×49. Longer steps make it worse, since growth is cosh ωT.

q: In the (x − p, ẋ) phase portrait, what happens on the line ẋ = −ω(x − p)?
choices: The CoM comes to rest exactly over p
The CoM runs away from p fastest
The CoM oscillates around p forever
The CoM crosses p and falls the other way
why: On that line only the e^(−ωt) part is present, so the CoM moves toward p at exactly the speed that stops it on top. ẋ = +ω(x − p) is the runaway line.

q: Starting anywhere off the rest line ẋ = −ω(x − p), what eventually happens to the LIPM?
choices: It runs away, to its side of the rest line
It settles back onto the rest line by itself
It runs away, always in the direction it was moving
It circles the origin of the phase plane forever
why: Every motion is a mix, and the e^(+ωt) part eventually wins. The side of the green line decides the direction of the fall, not the current velocity alone.

q: What is the capture point ξ?
choices: ξ = x + ẋ/ω: where to step to come to rest in one step
ξ = x − ẋ/ω: where to step to come to rest in one step
ξ = x + ẋ ω: where the CoM will be one step from now
ξ = p + ẋ/ω: how far the ZMP moves per time constant
why: ξ = x + ẋ/ω measures how far the state is from the rest line. x − ẋ/ω is the other combination η, which settles by itself.

q: The CoM is at x = 0, moving at 0.2 m/s, with ω = 4 /s. Where is the capture point?
choices: 0.05 m ahead
0.05 m behind
0.8 m ahead
0.2 m ahead
why: ξ = 0 + 0.2/4 = 0.05 m. Subtracting gives −0.05; multiplying by ω gives 0.8.

q: The CoM is at x = 0.1 m, moving at 0.5 m/s, with ω = 5 /s. Where is the capture point?
why: ξ = 0.1 + 0.5/5 = 0.2 m. x − ẋ/ω gives 0; x + ẋω gives 2.6; x + ẋ gives 0.6.

q: z_c = 0.4 m, g = 10 m/s², and the CoM moves at 0.3 m/s. How far ahead of the CoM is the capture point?
choices: 6 cm ahead
1.2 cm ahead
1.5 m ahead
6 cm behind
why: ω = √(10/0.4) = 5, so ẋ/ω = 0.3/5 = 0.06 m ahead. 1.2 cm uses ω = 25 (no root); 1.5 m multiplies by ω; behind is the x − ẋ/ω sign slip.

q: At one speed the capture point is 7.4 cm ahead of the CoM. The robot doubles its speed (same ω). Where is it now?
choices: About 15 cm ahead
About 7.4 cm ahead
About 30 cm ahead
About 10.5 cm ahead
why: ξ − x = ẋ/ω is linear in ẋ, so doubling the speed doubles it. 30 cm would be quadratic; 10.5 cm (×√2) has no basis.

q: The capture point obeys ξ̇ = ω(ξ − p). What does that mean?
choices: First order, and ξ − p grows like e^(ωt)
A second-order equation: ξ oscillates about p at frequency ω
A first-order equation: ξ decays onto p on its own
No dynamics at all: ξ is a constant of the motion
why: ξ(t) − p = (ξ0 − p)e^(ωt): the unstable part of the LIPM isolated in one variable. The combination that decays by itself is η = x − ẋ/ω.

q: ξ0 − p = 1 cm with p held fixed. After one time constant 1/ω, how far is ξ from p?
choices: About 2.7 cm
About 2 cm
About 1 cm
About 7 cm
why: ξ − p = (ξ0 − p)e^(ωt), and at t = 1/ω that is e ≈ 2.7 times. 7 is cosh 2.6, the per-step growth, not per time constant.

q: The foot (the ZMP) is put exactly on the capture point ξ. What happens?
choices: ξ stays put, and the CoM slides onto it and stops
The CoM stops at once, wherever it happens to be
The CoM runs away from ξ as fast as possible
The CoM oscillates around ξ until damping stops it
why: With p = ξ, ξ̇ = ω(ξ − p) = 0, so ξ is fixed and the state lies on the rest line. The CoM coasts onto the foot and comes to rest.

q: A robot steps well beyond its capture point. What happens, according to the LIPM?
choices: It is pushed back: the CoM stops short
It is safest: stepping further is always better
It stops exactly over the new foot
It keeps falling forward past the foot
why: Step short and you keep falling forward; step beyond and you are pushed back. Only stepping on ξ brings the CoM to rest in one step.

q: At 0.3 m/s with ω = 4.04 /s, where is the capture point, and what changes at twice the speed?
choices: 7.4 cm ahead; at twice the speed ~15 cm, more than the foot reaches
15 cm ahead; at twice the speed ~30 cm, more than the foot reaches
7.4 cm ahead; at twice the speed still within the 17 cm foot
1.2 cm ahead; at twice the speed 2.4 cm, inside the foot
why: 0.3/4.04 = 7.4 cm. Twice the speed needs ~15 cm, beyond the ~12 cm the foot reaches ahead of the ankle, so you must take a step.

q: How does the walker choose a step's initial CoM velocity v0?
choices: Solve a BVP so x(T) = x_T: exactly one answer
Integrate the LIPM backwards in time from the end of the step
Try several v0 values on the robot and keep the best one
Set v0 to the capture point so the step ends at rest
why: x_T = p + (x0 − p) cosh ωT + (v0/ω) sinh ωT is linear in v0, so it has one solution. No search or trial and error is needed.

q: The professor says to "run it backwards" to plan a step. What does that mean?
choices: Reason from the end you want to the start you need
Integrate the LIPM equation backwards in time
Play the recorded motion in reverse to check it
Walk the robot backwards to test its stability
why: It means the boundary value problem: fix x(T) and solve for v0. It is not integrating backwards in time.

q: With z_c = 0.6 m, the CoM must go from −0.07 m to +0.07 m in 0.65 s over a fixed ZMP. What v0 did the BVP give?
why: 0.14 m in 0.65 s averages 0.215 m/s, but the pendulum slows the CoM until it passes the foot, so it must start faster: 0.327 m/s. 0.416 m/s is the sideways v0.

q: How are the per-step boundary value problems combined into a gait?
choices: Chained: each step starts exactly where the last one ended
Solved independently, each from the robot's starting point
Averaged, so that every step uses the same v0
Solved once for the first step and then repeated
why: Each step's CoM trajectory must start where the previous one ended. Computing them absolutely breaks the continuity at every support exchange.

q: The robot falls at every support exchange, and the commanded pelvis jumps back half a stride there. What is the cause?
choices: Bookkeeping: steps computed absolutely, not chained
A balance problem: the ZMP leaves the support polygon at exchange
A damping problem: λ in the leg IK is too small
A gravity problem: ω is too large for this CoM height
why: Computing each step's trajectory absolutely teleports the body back half a stride. It looks like a balance failure and is bookkeeping.

q: For mirrored sideways steps (stance foot at ±w), where is the CoM at each support exchange?
choices: Exactly on the midline, y0 = 0
Directly over the new stance foot
Directly over the old stance foot
Halfway between midline and foot
why: Solving the periodic boundary problem forces y0 = −y0, so y0 = 0: the CoM crosses the midline at each support exchange, moving toward the new stance foot.

q: For the G1's sideways sway (w = 0.119 m), what are v0 at exchange and the sway's peak?
choices: v0 = 0.416 m/s, peak 5.9 cm
v0 = 0.327 m/s, peak 11.9 cm
v0 = 0.416 m/s, peak 11.9 cm
v0 = 0.110 m/s, peak 2.5 cm
why: v0 = ω w tanh(ωT/2) = 0.416 m/s, and the sway peaks at 5.9 cm. 0.327 m/s is the forward BVP's v0.

q: In the G1's periodic sway, does the CoM reach the foot it leans toward?
choices: No: it peaks at 5.9 cm against the foot at 11.9 cm
Yes: it must be over the foot to be balanced
Yes, but only during double support
No: it never leaves the midline at all
why: It never reaches the foot. Requiring the CoM over the foot is static walking; the dynamic gait only needs the ZMP there.

q: The swing foot follows x = x_A + (x_B − x_A)(σ − sin 2πσ / 2π). Why that shape?
choices: Its speed factor 1 − cos 2πσ is 0 at both ends
It is the shortest path from x_A to x_B
It keeps the foot speed constant all the way
It makes the foot accelerate fastest at landing
why: Zero velocity at σ = 0 and σ = 1: the foot leaves gently and lands at rest. A straight line would jump to full speed at once.

q: Why not swing the foot along a straight line, x_A + (x_B − x_A)σ?
choices: It starts at full speed and lands still sliding
It is just as good; the cycloid only looks nicer
It is too slow to finish within one step
It makes the foot rise too high at mid-swing
why: A linear blend has constant speed from the first instant: a jolt the servos cannot follow and a foot still moving when it lands.

q: Swing height z = z0 + h(1 − cos 2πσ)/2 with h = 0.10 m. How high above z0 is the foot at σ = 0.25?
choices: 0 m

q: Double-support fraction d = 0.20 at each end, swing fraction σ = (s − d)/(1 − 2d). What is σ at step fraction s = 0.35?
Which is the walker's pipeline, run every cycle at 500 Hz?
choices: Time → step → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → DLS IK → 29 servos → physics
IMU → state estimate → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → DLS IK → servos
Time → DLS IK → LIPM CoM target → foot targets → 29 servos → physics
Contact forces → ZMP → capture point → foot targets → 29 servos → physics
why: It is open loop: nothing comes back from the physics, no IMU, no measured ZMP. The IK comes after the CoM and foot targets, since it turns them into angles.

q: What are the walker's default gait parameters?
choices: Step 0.14 m, 0.65 s, clearance 0.10 m, 20 % double support
Step 0.65 m, 0.14 s, clearance 0.20 m, 10 % double support
Step 0.14 m, 0.45 s, clearance 0.10 m, no double support
Step 0.30 m, 0.65 s, clearance 0.05 m, 50 % double support
why: 0.14 m strides, 0.65 s per step, 10 cm swing clearance, 20 % double support at each end. 0.45 s steps are the rushed gait that falls.

q: Why is the walker's first step only a half stride?
choices: Both feet start level, so a full stride would over-reach
The LIPM needs one half step to measure ω
The servos must warm up before full strides
The capture point starts behind the heels
why: Each later forward BVP runs from half a stride behind the stance foot to half ahead. Starting with feet level, the first step only needs to cover half.

q: Someone pushes the walking G1 sideways mid-walk. What does the analytic walker do?
choices: Nothing different: it is open loop and never reads the IMU
It steps onto its new capture point to catch itself
It shifts its ZMP with ankle torque to recover
It slows its gait until the sway dies away
why: The walker never measures where the body is; it cannot see the push, so it cannot react. Catching it would need feedback, e.g. capture-point stepping.

q: Which list gives the open-loop walker's limitations?
choices: Drifts sideways, no push recovery, flat ground, fixed gait
Slips on ice, needs learning, cannot turn, drains the battery
Too slow to compute, singular at the crouch, falls on the Moon
Needs an IMU, needs a camera, needs 150 million steps
why: Nothing pulls it back, nothing reacts to disturbances, and the gait is fixed at design time. Ice (friction 0.2) actually changes nothing for this gait.

q: Why did the field move from planned walkers like this one to feedback?
choices: A plan made in advance is brittle outside its conditions
Because the LIPM mathematics turned out to be wrong
Because analytic walkers cannot walk at all in practice
Because learned policies need far fewer simulation steps
why: The maths works, as the walker shows; but an open-loop plan cannot respond to pushes, drift or terrain. Learned policies need far more steps (~150 million), not fewer.

q: Why can the ZMP not jump instantly from one foot to the other?
choices: Non-negative weighted average: between feet only while both touch
The servos are too slow to shift the weight from one foot to the other in a single cycle
The LIPM forbids any change of p within a step, since p is held fixed in the solution
The CoM must first pass over the new foot, and that takes one whole time constant
why: With only one foot touching, all the weight is there; the ZMP can travel between the feet only during double support. That is why the gait spends 20 % of each step there.

q: Is double support essential for the G1 walker, or just a nicety?
choices: Essential: with double_support = 0 it falls at 2.0 s
A nicety: it only makes the gait look smoother
Harmful: removing it makes the gait more stable
Irrelevant: the ZMP can switch feet instantly
why: Without it the ZMP must switch feet in an instant, the step starts with an error, and errors grow ×7 per step. Measured: a fall at 2.0 s.

q: How far and how fast did the analytic G1 walker go?
choices: 0.99 m in 8.8 s, about 0.11 m/s
8.8 m in 0.99 s, about 9 m/s
0.65 m in 8.8 s, about 0.07 m/s
0.99 m in 2.0 s, about 0.5 m/s
why: Walked 0.99 m in 8.8 s with no learning and ~200 lines of code: 0.99/8.8 ≈ 0.11 m/s. 2.0 s is when the no-double-support gait falls.

q: What made the week 4 G1 walk?
choices: One linear ODE, its exact solution, a cycloid and IK
A neural network policy trained for 150 million simulation steps
A reward function tuned by search in MuJoCo over many runs
Motion-capture data from human walkers, replayed through IK
why: No training, no data, no reward function: roughly two hundred lines of analytic control (Layer 4) doing the whole job.

q: Within what band did the G1's pelvis height stay during the walk?
why: The crouched gait kept the pelvis in 0.69–0.74 m throughout, and it ended upright at 0.716 m. A lower band would mean a deep squat; the 0.13 m figure is a collapsed robot.

q: When did the failure variants of the walker fall?
choices: No double support 2.0 s; rushed 3.2 s; Moon 5.3 s; ice never
No double support 5.3 s; rushed 2.0 s; Moon 3.2 s; ice 8.8 s
No double support 3.2 s; rushed 5.3 s; Moon 2.0 s; ice never
All four fell at the first support exchange, about 1.0 s
why: Measured with walk.py: double_support = 0 at 2.0 s, 0.45 s steps at 3.2 s, Moon gravity at 5.3 s; ice (friction 0.2) changes nothing for this gait.

q: The walker is put on ice (friction 0.2) without telling the controller. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes for this gait
It slips and falls at the first step
It falls at 2.0 s, like no double support
It walks, but only half as far
why: Measured: ice (friction 0.2) changes nothing for this gait. Friction only caps how hard the floor can push sideways, and this gait stays within that cap.

q: On the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s², z_c = 0.6 m), ω ≈ 1.6 /s instead of 4.04 /s. How does the time constant change?
choices: About 2.5 times longer: ~0.6 s instead of 0.25 s
About 2.5 times shorter: ~0.1 s instead of 0.25 s
About 6 times longer: ~1.5 s instead of 0.25 s
Unchanged: the time constant depends only on z_c
why: 1/ω goes from 0.247 s to about 0.61 s, a ratio of √(9.81/1.62) ≈ 2.5. 6 is the ratio of the g values, which forgets the square root.

q: The measured ZMP leaves the support polygon while the G1 walks. What does the course conclude?
choices: The ZMP criterion is right; the LIPM's assumptions failed
The ZMP criterion is wrong for real humanoid robots
The contact-force measurement must have a bug in it
The robot is about to fall, since the ZMP is outside
why: Theory says flat feet cannot put the ZMP outside; the real robot breaks the model's assumptions (swinging leg, bobbing CoM, heavy legs, rolling feet, sagging servos). Teach it; do not "fix" it.

q: Over the walk, where did the measured ZMP y range, against stance feet at ±0.119 m?
why: From about −0.23 to +0.11 m, beyond the −0.119 m foot on one side. −0.12 to +0.10 m is just one early step's row from the printout.

q: Which real-robot fact breaks the LIPM's massless-leg assumption?
choices: About 30 % of the G1's mass is below the hips
The servos have finite stiffness and sag
The CoM bobs as the stance leg compresses
The weight rolls across a finite-size foot
why: All four are listed failures, but only the heavy legs contradict "massless legs". Sagging servos break rigid control, bobbing breaks constant height, rolling breaks instant exchange.

q: Complete the professor's line: "A model does not have to be true to be useful, only …"
choices: … wrong in ways that do not matter yet.
… simple enough to solve by hand.
… right on average over many steps.
… tuned on the real robot's data.
why: The LIPM is wrong about the G1 in five ways and the robot still walks. Weeks 11 and 12 are where those errors start to matter.

q: A learned walking policy may need 150 million simulation steps. What does the course say learning buys?
choices: Robustness, not the gait itself
The gait itself, which analytic control cannot produce
Speed: learned gaits are always faster to compute
Nothing that analytic control cannot match
why: An analytic controller already walks in ~200 lines with no data. "Learning buys robustness, not the gait itself."

q: On the G1, what torque does MuJoCo's position actuator actually compute?
choices: τ = k_p(q_ref − q) − k_v·q̇, a PD law
τ = k_p(q_ref − q) + k_i∫e dt, a PI law
τ = k_p(q_ref − q) alone, a pure spring
none: it sets q = q_ref exactly each step
why: The 'position actuator' is a PD controller written into the model file: a spring toward the command plus a damper on velocity. It is not an ideal servo that teleports the joint, and it has no integral term.

q: The position actuator sits on a seam between two layers of the stack. Which?
choices: Declared in Layer 2 (robot model), doing Layer 4's (control) job
Declared in Layer 4 (control), doing Layer 1's (physics) job
Declared in Layer 5 (AI), doing Layer 4's (control) job
Declared in Layer 1 (physics), doing Layer 2's (model) job
why: The actuator is written in the MJCF (Layer 2), but what it declares is a feedback controller, which is Layer 4's job. That is why the guide calls it 'a controller in disguise'.

q: In τ = k_p(q_ref − q) − k_v·q̇, what does the D term do while the joint is moving TOWARD its target?
choices: Brakes it anyway: it opposes motion in either direction
Speeds it up, adding torque toward the target
Nothing: it acts only when moving away from the target
Reverses sign so that it helps the P term pull
why: −k_v·q̇ depends only on the velocity, not on the error, so it resists any motion, even motion toward the target. Thinking D 'helps' the joint arrive is the common slip.

q: In the spring–damper picture of the servo, what are the spring and the damper attached to?
choices: Spring to the command; damper to the ground
Spring to the ground; damper to the command
Both to the command, so both move with ctrl
Both to the ground, so neither moves with ctrl
why: Moving ctrl drags the spring's end (the P term pulls toward the command), while the damper is fixed to the ground, so it brakes all motion. Swapping them would make the damper oppose only motion relative to the command.

q: MuJoCo's general actuator is τ = g0·ctrl + b0 + b1·q + b2·q̇. Which settings make it the PD position servo?
why: Collecting terms gives k_p·ctrl − k_p·q − k_v·q̇ = k_p(ctrl − q) − k_v·q̇. So k_p appears twice (gain and bias); leaving b1 = 0 would give a torque that does not depend on q at all.

q: To make a servo stiffer you change only gainprm[0] (g0) from 500 to 1000 and leave biasprm alone. What happens?
choices: It now pulls toward a different angle than ctrl
It is twice as stiff and still pulls toward ctrl
Nothing: only biasprm sets the stiffness
The damping doubles; the stiffness is unchanged
why: k_p appears twice (g0 and b1 = −k_p). With g0 = 1000 and b1 = −500 the torque is zero at q = 2·ctrl, so the servo aims at the wrong angle. That is why scale_gains writes three numbers.

q: An actuator has g0 = 1000, b1 = −500, b0 = b2 = 0 (gravity off). With ctrl = 0.1 rad, where does the joint come to rest?
choices: q = 0.2 rad
q = 0.1 rad
q = 0.05 rad
q = 0.4 rad
why: At rest τ = 0: 1000·0.1 − 500·q = 0, so q = 100/500 = 0.2 rad. It would be 0.1 rad only if g0 and −b1 were equal, as in a real position actuator.

q: How do the G1's servo gains vary across its joints?
choices: k_p = 500 everywhere; k_v ranges about 4.55 to 43
k_v = 500 everywhere; k_p ranges about 4.55 to 43
k_p = 500 on the legs, 100 on the arms; k_v fixed
k_p ranges 250 to 1000; k_v = 15.85 everywhere
why: Stiffness is uniform (500) and damping is not: k_v spans roughly tenfold, 4.55 to 43. 15.85 is the knee's k_v alone, and 250/1000 are the sweep values that fall.

q: One servoed joint, gravity off, other joints held still. Which equation does it obey?
choices: M·q̈ + k_v·q̇ + k_p·q = k_p·q_ref
M·q̈ + k_p·q̇ + k_v·q = k_v·q_ref
M·q̇ + k_v·q = k_p·q_ref
M·q̈ = k_p·q_ref − k_v·q
why: Newton for rotation (M·q̈ = τ) with the PD torque, unknowns moved left: the mass–spring–damper equation. It is second order, with damping on q̇ and stiffness on q; the swapped version mixes up k_p and k_v.

q: In the one-joint model M·q̈ + k_v·q̇ + k_p·q = k_p·q_ref, what is M for the knee?
choices: Inertia of everything beyond the joint about its axis, plus armature
The total mass of the robot, about 33 kg, felt equally by every joint
The rotor inertia of the knee motor alone, read from its datasheet
The inertia of the bodies on the pelvis side of the knee, thigh up
why: M is the joint's diagonal entry of the mass matrix (mj_fullM): what the knee must swing (shin and foot), plus the motor's armature (0.01 kg·m² on G1 leg joints). It is not the whole robot's mass and not the bodies on the pelvis side.

q: Substituting e = e^(rt) into M·ë + k_v·ė + k_p·e = 0 gives which characteristic equation?
choices: M·r² + k_v·r + k_p = 0
k_p·r² + k_v·r + M = 0
M·r² + k_p·r + k_v = 0
r² + k_v·r + k_p·M = 0
why: Each derivative brings down one r: M·r²·e^(rt) + k_v·r·e^(rt) + k_p·e^(rt) = 0, then cancel e^(rt). The inertia goes with r², the damping with r, the stiffness alone.

q: Matching M·r² + k_v·r + k_p = 0 to r² + 2ζω_n·r + ω_n² = 0 gives which ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = k_p/M, ζ = k_v/(2·k_p·M)
ω_n = √(k_p·M), ζ = k_v/√(k_p/M)
why: Divide by M: ω_n² = k_p/M and 2ζω_n = k_v/M, so ζ = k_v/(2Mω_n) = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)). Forgetting the square root or the 2 are the usual slips.

q: k_p = 400 N·m/rad, M = 1 kg·m², k_v = 40 N·m·s/rad. What are ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 1.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 2.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
why: ω_n = √(400/1) = 20; ζ = 40/(2·√400) = 40/40 = 1.0, critically damped. Dropping the 2 gives ζ = 2; skipping the root gives ω_n = 400.

q: k_p = 100, M = 4 kg·m², k_v = 10. What are ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 5 rad/s, ζ = 0.25
ω_n = 5 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
why: ω_n = √(100/4) = 5; ζ = 10/(2·√400) = 10/40 = 0.25, so it rings (about 44 % overshoot). ζ = 0.5 comes from forgetting the 2; ω_n = 20 is √(k_p·M) instead of √(k_p/M).

q: Practice Q14: k_p = 900, M = 1 kg·m², k_v = 30. What are ω_n and ζ, and does it overshoot?
choices: ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 16 %
ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 1.0; no overshoot
ω_n = 900 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 16 %
ω_n = 30 rad/s, ζ = 0.5; yes, about 44 %
why: ω_n = √900 = 30; ζ = 30/(2·30) = 0.5, under-damped, overshoot exp(−π·0.5/√0.75) ≈ 16 %. 44 % belongs to ζ = 0.25; ζ = 1.0 forgets the 2.

q: k_p = 400, M = 0.25 kg·m². Which k_v makes the joint critically damped (ζ = 1)?
choices: 20 N·m·s/rad
10 N·m·s/rad
40 N·m·s/rad
100 N·m·s/rad
why: ζ = 1 means k_v = 2√(k_p·M) = 2√100 = 20. 10 forgets the 2; 100 is k_p·M without the root.

q: k_p = 200, M = 2 kg·m². Which k_v gives ζ = 1?
choices: 40 N·m·s/rad
20 N·m·s/rad
400 N·m·s/rad
10 N·m·s/rad
why: k_v = 2√(k_p·M) = 2√400 = 2·20 = 40. 20 is √(k_p·M) without the 2; 400 is k_p·M with no root; 10 would be 2√(k_p/M).

q: For ζ < 1, what are the characteristic roots and what does the joint do?
choices: A complex pair −ζω_n ± iω_d: it overshoots and rings
A double real root −ω_n: fastest arrival with no overshoot
Two different negative real roots: it creeps in slowly
A pair with positive real part: the joint diverges
why: Below ζ = 1 the square root √(ζ² − 1) is imaginary, so the roots are complex: decay times oscillation, i.e. ringing. The double root is ζ = 1 and two real roots is ζ > 1; with k_v > 0 nothing diverges.

q: What does critical damping (ζ = 1) give a joint's step response?
choices: The fastest arrival without any overshoot
The fastest arrival of any ζ, with slight overshoot
Zero steady-state sag under a gravity load
The slowest arrival, but with the least torque
why: ζ = 1 is the double root −ω_n: the quickest response that never passes the target. Lower ζ can get near the target sooner but overshoots; ζ says nothing about sag, which is τ_g/k_p.

q: An over-damped joint (ζ > 1) has two real negative roots. Which one decides how long you wait?
choices: The slow root, the one nearer zero
The fast root, the one farther from zero
Their average, which is −ζω_n
Neither: it always arrives in 1/ω_n
why: e(t) is a sum of two decaying exponentials; the fast one dies in milliseconds and the slow one is what you wait for. At ζ = 4 on the knee that slow root is −8 /s, five times slower than critical.

q: With k_v > 0 and k_p > 0, what is guaranteed about a joint's step response?
choices: It always arrives; only the way it arrives changes
It arrives only if ζ ≥ 1; below that it rings for ever
It arrives only if ζ ≤ 1; above that it stalls short
It arrives only if k_p is larger than k_v
why: With k_v > 0 both roots have negative real part, so every term decays: 'the joint always arrives; the question is how'. Ringing decays, and over-damped creeping still converges.

q: For an under-damped joint, what is the magnitude of each complex root?
choices: Exactly ω_n
Exactly ζ·ω_n
Exactly ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²)
Exactly 2ζ·ω_n
why: |r|² = (ζω_n)² + ω_d² = ω_n²(ζ² + 1 − ζ²) = ω_n². So damping slides the pair around a circle of radius ω_n; ζω_n is only the real part and ω_d only the imaginary part.

q: ω_n = 10 rad/s and ζ = 0.6. What are the characteristic roots?
why: Real part −ζω_n = −6; imaginary part ω_d = ω_n√(1 − 0.36) = 10·0.8 = 8. Check: |−6 + 8i| = 10 = ω_n. Using ω_n itself as the imaginary part gives −6 ± 10i.

q: The one-joint step response's overshoot, exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)), depends on what?
choices: ζ only
ω_n only: quicker joints overshoot more
The step size: bigger steps overshoot more
k_p alone, whatever the damping
why: The formula contains nothing but ζ, so two joints with very different speeds but the same ζ overshoot by the same fraction. Stiffness changes the overshoot only through ζ.

q: What overshoot does exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) give at ζ = 0.25, 0.5 and 1?
why: ζ = 0.25 gives 44 %, ζ = 0.5 gives 16 %, and at ζ = 1 the peak time is infinite, so there is no overshoot. 56 % is the measured P-only knee, a different experiment.

q: Complete the professor's line: 'Stiffness sets the ___; the damping ratio sets the ___.'
choices: speed; shape
shape; speed
sag; speed
torque; sag
why: ω_n = √(k_p/M) sets how fast the joint responds; ζ alone sets whether it overshoots (the shape). The reversed version is the tempting misremembering.

q: A joint has ω_n = 10 rad/s and ζ = 1. You quadruple k_p, keeping M and k_v. What are the new ω_n and ζ?
choices: ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.5
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 1.0
ω_n = 20 rad/s, ζ = 2.0
why: ω_n ∝ √k_p doubles to 20, and ζ = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)) ∝ 1/√k_p halves to 0.5. Scaling linearly (×4, ÷4) or assuming ζ is unchanged are the slips.

q: A critically damped joint is made 4× stiffer (k_p × 4, k_v unchanged) to respond faster. What happens to its shape?
choices: ζ halves to 0.5, so it now overshoots (≈16 % by formula)
ζ stays 1.0, because ζ depends only on k_v and M
ζ doubles to 2, so it becomes sluggish and creeps in
ζ drops to 0.25, so it overshoots by about 44 %
why: ζ = k_v/(2√(k_p·M)) contains k_p under a root, so ×4 stiffness halves ζ. Quadrupling k_p doubles the speed AND halves ζ; to keep ζ = 1 you would have to double k_v too.

q: On the lifted G1 knee (0.5 rad step), what did k_p × 4 do compared with the shipped gains?
choices: 1 % in 0.032 s vs 0.110 s; 4 % overshoot; 1000 N·m peak
1 % in 0.220 s vs 0.110 s; no overshoot; 250 N·m peak
1 % in 0.032 s vs 0.110 s; no overshoot; 250 N·m peak
Never within 1 % in 0.5 s: it became over-damped
why: ×4 stiffness doubles ω_n and halves ζ to 0.5, so it arrives about 3.4× sooner, pays a 4.0 % overshoot, and draws 4× the torque (k_p × 0.5 rad = 1000 N·m). Over-damped is what k_p ÷ 4 does.

q: Just after a 0.5 rad step, the error is the whole step. What is the initial torque at k_p = 500, and at k_p = 2000?
choices: 250 N·m and 1000 N·m
250 N·m and 500 N·m
500 N·m and 2000 N·m
1000 N·m and 4000 N·m
why: τ = k_p·e at q̇ = 0: 500·0.5 = 250 N·m and 2000·0.5 = 1000 N·m. Torque scales linearly with k_p, not with √k_p, so a 4× stiffer servo draws 4× the torque.

q: Why does the G1's k_v vary about tenfold across the leg joints while k_p is 500 on all of them?
choices: Each leg joint is set to ζ = 1, so k_v = 2√(k_p·M) tracks M
Each leg joint is set to the same ω_n, so k_v must cancel M
k_v was hand-tuned per joint to minimise sag during the walk
Heavier joints need more stiffness, and k_v is what supplies it
why: Solving ζ = 1 for the damping gives k_v = 2√(k_p·M): same k_p, different M, different k_v. So the heavy hip and the light ankle respond with the same shape. Damping has no effect on sag.

q: What damping ratio do the G1's twelve leg joints have, and its arm joints?
choices: Legs all ζ = 1.00; arms looser, 0.7–1.9
Legs all ζ = 0.5; arms all ζ = 1.00
Legs spread 0.7–1.9; arms all ζ = 1.00
Legs all ζ = 0.25; arms all ζ = 4
why: Read M off the mass matrix and compute ζ: every leg joint is exactly critically damped, while the arms spread 0.7–1.9. The legs got the design rule; the arms did not.

q: For the G1 knee (M ≈ 0.126 kg·m², k_p = 500), what is ω_n?
choices: About 63 rad/s, roughly 10 Hz
About 4000 rad/s, roughly 630 Hz
About 10 rad/s, roughly 1.6 Hz
About 63 Hz, roughly 400 rad/s
why: √(500/0.126) ≈ √4000 ≈ 63 rad/s, and 63/(2π) ≈ 10 Hz: an undamped knee would ring ten times a second. 4000 is ω_n² (forgot the root); '63 Hz' confuses rad/s with Hz.

q: For the G1 knee, what are its basic time unit 1/ω_n and the time critical damping takes to get within 1 %?
choices: About 16 ms; about 0.1 s (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
About 0.1 s; about 0.6 s (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
About 16 ms; about 16 ms (one time unit)
About 1.6 ms; about 10 ms (≈ 6.6/ω_n)
why: 1/63 ≈ 16 ms, and (1 + x)e^(−x) = 0.01 at x ≈ 6.6, so critical damping needs about seven time units ≈ 0.105 s. It does not arrive in one time unit.

q: A critically damped joint gets within 1 % after about 6.6/ω_n. For ω_n = 20 rad/s, how long is that?
choices: About 0.33 s
About 0.05 s
About 1.05 s
About 3.0 s
why: 6.6/20 = 0.33 s. 0.05 s is one time unit 1/ω_n; 1.05 s would come from dividing by 2π instead of ω_n.

q: The knee with k_v × 4 (ζ = 4): what are its roots, and how long to reach 1 %?
choices: −8 and −497 /s; about 0.58 s, set by the slow root
−63 and −63 /s; about 0.1 s, as fast as critical
−16 ± 61i /s; about 0.03 s, with 44 % overshoot
−8 and −497 /s; about 0.02 s, set by the fast root
why: Over-damped: two real roots whose product is ω_n² (8 × 497 ≈ 63²). The fast one dies in milliseconds; the slow e^(−8t) is what you wait for, about 0.577 s.

q: On the G1 lifted clear of the floor, k_v/4 on the knee overshot 16.9 %, but the one-joint formula predicts 44 %. Why?
choices: The other joints and the floating pelvis move back; nothing is a wall
MuJoCo's integrator adds numerical damping that eats the ringing
The formula is wrong: overshoot really depends on ω_n as well
The 0.3 N·m joint friction absorbs most of the swing energy
why: The one-joint model assumes every other joint is welded still; in a floating robot the knee pushes against a body that gives way, so less inertia and relatively more damping. The formula is right about direction and design rule, only approximate in numbers.

q: What does the guide say to do with the one-joint formula on a whole robot?
choices: Use it to choose gains; measure to know what you got
Trust it over measurement, since simulation is approximate
Use it only on the arms; legs need the full mass matrix
Discard it on a humanoid and tune gains by trial alone
why: It over-predicts ringing (44 % vs 16.9 %) but its design rule (ζ = 1, no overshoot) holds. The course's thread is 'measure, do not believe', so the formula guides and the measurement decides.

q: With k_v/4 on the knee of the lifted G1, the one-joint formula predicts 44 % overshoot. What did the real robot do?
choices: Rang less, 16.9 %: the rest of the body gives way
Exactly 44 %, just as the one-joint formula predicts
Rang more, about 56 %: the pelvis adds extra inertia
No overshoot at all, since the legs are critically damped
why: The formula OVER-predicts ringing on the real robot (16.9 % measured vs 44 %), because the other joints and the floating pelvis move back. k_v/4 makes ζ = 0.25, so the joint is no longer critically damped.

q: At rest under a gravity torque τ_g, the servo balances 0 = k_p(q_ref − q) + τ_g. What is the sag?
choices: q − q_ref = τ_g/k_p
q − q_ref = τ_g·k_p
q − q_ref = τ_g/k_v
q − q_ref = τ_g/(k_p + k_v)
why: At rest q̇ = 0, so the damper contributes nothing and the spring alone holds the load: deflection = load ÷ stiffness. Damping cannot appear in it.

q: A servo with k_p = 300 N·m/rad holds a 6 N·m gravity load. How large is the steady sag?
choices: 0.02 rad
0.2 rad
0.05 rad
why: τ_g/k_p = 6/300 = 0.02 rad (about 1.1°). The sag shrinks as k_p grows; multiplying instead of dividing is the classic slip.

q: Practice Q3: k_p = 400 holds a joint against 8 N·m of gravity. What is the steady error, and what if k_p is doubled?
choices: 0.02 rad, then 0.01 rad
0.02 rad, then 0.04 rad
0.02 rad, then exactly zero
0.05 rad, then 0.025 rad
why: 8/400 = 0.02 rad; doubling k_p halves it to 0.01 rad, never zero, because a PD spring needs an error to make the holding torque.

q: Which change removes the steady gravity sag of a servo completely?
choices: Adding an integral (I) term
Raising k_p as high as possible
Raising k_v until it is over-damped
Setting the damping ratio to exactly 1
why: Only the I term remembers the past and keeps growing until the error is zero; on the knee it ended up carrying the whole 10 N·m. A finite k_p only shrinks the sag, and damping changes how it arrives, not where.

q: 'With a stiff enough PD servo, the sag goes to zero.' Why is this wrong?
choices: Sag is τ_g/k_p: halved by doubling k_p, but never zero
Sag is τ_g/k_v: only the damper sets it, not k_p
Sag grows with k_p, since a stiffer spring takes more load
Sag is fixed by ζ, so stiffness changes the shape only
why: The error is what produces the holding torque, so a finite spring must deflect. 'A spring at rest is a spring under load, and load means deflection.'

q: 'A spring at rest is a spring under load, and load means deflection.' What does this line explain?
choices: Why a PD servo holding a weight sits off its command
Why a joint overshoots when its damping is too low
Why the hand-written servo blows up at 500 Hz
Why the CPG falls despite a plausible step pattern
why: The servo is a spring, and a spring only pushes when stretched; holding gravity therefore needs a steady error τ_g/k_p. That is the sag, not ringing or numerical instability.

q: How much steady pelvis sag does the whole walking G1 have at k_p = 500?
choices: About 11 mm
About 11 cm
About 0.11 mm
Exactly zero
why: Each leg joint sags by its own τ_g/k_p and those small angles add up along the leg to about 11 mm. Not a bug: the necessary deflection of finite springs holding up a 33 kg robot.

q: The G1's arm held straight out loads its shoulder with 4.7 N·m at k_p = 500. How much does it sag?
choices: About 9.5 mrad, half a degree
About 95 mrad, over 5 degrees
About 0.95 mrad, a twentieth of a degree
About 20 mrad, over a degree
why: 4.7/500 ≈ 9.4 mrad, and the measured 9.5 mrad lands on τ_g/k_p within 0.05 mrad (about 3.6 mm at the wrist). 20 mrad is the knee experiment's 10 N·m load.

q: The G1's joints have frictionloss 0.3 N·m. What does that do to the sag at k_p = 500?
choices: A dead band: rest may be up to 0.6 mrad either side of τ_g/k_p
It removes the sag, since friction holds the load instead
It doubles the sag, since friction adds to the gravity torque
Nothing: friction acts only when the joint moves fast
why: Friction can hold up to 0.3 N·m either way, so the spring may rest anywhere within ±0.3/k_p = ±0.6 mrad of the prediction. It neither removes nor doubles the sag.

q: In τ = k_p·e + k_i∫e dt + k_d·ė, which term reacts to what?
choices: P to the present, I to the past, D to the trend
P to the past, I to the trend, D to the present
P to the trend, I to the present, D to the past
P to the present, I to the trend, D to the past
why: P uses the error now, I accumulates error over time (it remembers), D uses how fast the error changes (it brakes before the target).
